about: Doctrine timelines, v2.8. All map cases have at least one doctrinal membership; three course chronologies separately index every source case. Each line has an authored guide explaining branches and relationship to earlier law. Summary means synthesis of the selected sources, not certification of all current law. Model UCC texts and Restatements are distinguished from enacted statutes. Turn labels may be replaced by a precise effect label. Audit basis and source locators are in tools/v25/timeline-audit.json and tools/content-audit/2026-11-17-corrections.json.

timelines.title: Consideration: what makes a promise a bargain?
timelines.question: What must someone give or promise in exchange for an enforceable promise?
timelines.anchor: what counts as consideration
timelines.now: Consideration is the performance or promise sought in exchange. It need not benefit the promisor or be an equal economic trade. An implied duty can make an apparently optional promise binding; surrendering a disputed claim can also count. The cases apply different jurisdictions’ rules, and the Restatement organizes those rules without enacting them.

steps.note: Detriment, not benefit: giving up a lawful freedom at the promisor's request is consideration whether or not the promisor gains anything.
steps.effect: Giving up a legal freedom

steps.note: An exclusive agent's implied promise of reasonable efforts keeps the deal from being illusory and supplies consideration (New York).
steps.effect: Finding an implied efforts promise

steps.note: The wife did not establish an enforceable bargain in this English family-support arrangement.
steps.effect: No established family bargain
steps.context: The judges gave different reasons. Atkin emphasized the lack of intent to create legal obligations; the opinions should not be collapsed into one universal rule about families.

steps.note: Giving up a claim that proves invalid is consideration if it was asserted with an honest and reasonable belief in its validity (Maryland).
steps.effect: Settling an honestly disputed claim

steps.note: Mattei’s promise was binding because he had to judge the proposed leases honestly, not reject them at will.
steps.effect: Constraining satisfaction with good faith
steps.context: For these varied leasing judgments, California used subjective good faith. The opinion separately identifies an objective reasonable-person test for commercial quality or utility.

steps.note: Second Restatement: consideration is a bargained-for exchange (§ 71), and a surrendered claim counts if doubtful or honestly believed (§ 74).
steps.effect: Defining bargain and surrendered claims

steps.note: Iowa adopts § 74: a claim later shown invalid still supports a settlement if it was doubtful or the claimant honestly believed it might be valid.
steps.effect: Protecting good-faith settlements

steps.note: A requirements contract has consideration even before the buyer has any requirements: § 2-306 binds it to buy its good-faith needs (Missouri law).
steps.effect: Committing to good-faith requirements

timelines.guide: Compare three kinds of exchange: giving up a legal freedom (Hamer), making an implied commitment (Wood and Mattei), and settling a disputed claim (Fiege and Dyer). Balfour asks a different threshold question: did this family arrangement create a legal bargain?

timelines.title: Good faith: discretion and promised efforts
timelines.question: What limits a party’s freedom to use contractual discretion?
timelines.anchor: the duty of good faith read into a contract
timelines.now: Good faith concerns how contractual duties are performed and enforced. It can constrain discretion without making one party responsible for the other’s interests. The duty’s scope depends on the contract and governing law. UCC § 1-304 covers every contract or duty within the Code; Restatement § 205 states a common-law formulation.

steps.note: Cardozo reads a duty of reasonable efforts into an exclusive agency: courts supply the obligation the business arrangement implies.
steps.effect: Implying reasonable efforts

steps.note: For goods, § 2-306 separates good-faith quantities from best efforts in an exclusive dealing arrangement.
steps.effect: Requiring efforts and good-faith quantities
steps.context: Subsection (1) measures output or requirements by good faith and limits disproportionate quantities. Subsection (2) requires best efforts in exclusive dealing unless the parties agree otherwise.

steps.note: Best efforts does not demand ruinous losses, but a brewer may not neglect the brand it promised to promote to raise its overall profit (New York law).
steps.effect: Enforcing brand-specific best efforts

steps.note: The Second Restatement states a duty of good faith in performance and enforcement. It is persuasive common-law authority; a jurisdiction must adopt or apply the proposition.
steps.effect: Stating a performance duty

steps.note: Posner: good faith forbids deliberately exploiting the other side's oversight about its contract rights, though it does not require altruism.
steps.effect: Examining deliberate exploitation

steps.note: A party must actually exercise a discretion it promised to exercise, and not arbitrarily, but good faith adds no duty the contract excludes (New York).
steps.effect: Requiring genuine consideration

steps.note: Singapore declines to imply a general duty of good faith in law; a term is implied in fact only where necessary.
steps.effect: Rejecting a general implied duty

steps.note: Federal airline law preempted this state-imposed good-faith claim.
steps.effect: Preempting this airline covenant claim
steps.context: The claim concerned airline prices, routes or services and added duties beyond the airline’s voluntary promises. Claims enforcing ordinary contractual promises present a separate question.

timelines.guide: Wood and Bloor concern promised efforts. Market Street and Dalton concern how a party uses existing contract rights. Read Ng Giap as a Singapore comparison and Ginsberg as a federal limit on an airline claim.

timelines.title: Promissory estoppel: promises people rely on
timelines.question: Can reliance make a promise enforceable without a bargain?
timelines.anchor: when reliance makes a promise enforceable
timelines.now: Under the Restatement § 90 approach, a promise can bind when reliance was expected, actually occurred, and enforcement is necessary to avoid injustice. The remedy may be limited. State adoption and other requirements still matter: reliance does not automatically create a final contract, guarantee expected profits, or satisfy a writing requirement.

steps.note: Alabama refused to enforce this promised home despite the relative’s costly move in reliance.
steps.effect: Refusing to enforce a gift
steps.context: The court treated the promise as a gratuity. Compare the later reliance-based cases; this historical result is not a statement that moving in reliance can never support enforcement.

steps.note: Equitable estoppel bars the no-consideration defense when the promisor induced the promisee to give up her job in reliance on his note (Nebraska).
steps.effect: Enforcing a promise after reliance

steps.note: The First Restatement states a route to enforcing promises that induce expected, substantial reliance.
steps.effect: Stating the first reliance formulation
steps.context: Its § 90 requires expected and actual action or forbearance of a definite and substantial character, with enforcement necessary to avoid injustice. This is the 1932 formulation.

steps.note: Reasonable reliance on the subcontractor’s bid protected time to accept it after the general contract was awarded.
steps.effect: Protecting time to accept a bid
steps.context: Using the bid did not itself create a subcontract. Protection can fail if the contractor knew or should have known of a mistake when relying, or later shopped the bid while trying to hold the offer open.

steps.note: A pension promise binds under § 90 because the employee retired in reliance on it, though her past service was no consideration (Missouri).
steps.effect: Enforcing a retirement promise

steps.note: Wisconsin applies § 90 to failed franchise negotiations: reliance losses are recoverable though the promises were too indefinite for a contract.
steps.effect: Protecting reliance during negotiations

steps.note: The Second Restatement revises the reliance test and allows the remedy to be limited as justice requires.
steps.effect: Revising the reliance formulation
steps.context: It removes “definite and substantial” and dispenses with proof of induced reliance for charitable subscriptions and marriage settlements. These proposed rules depend on jurisdictional adoption.

steps.note: Reliance on an at-will assurance earns reliance damages, such as a lost sale price, not the profits the relationship would have brought (Indiana law).
steps.effect: Compensating a lost sale opportunity

steps.note: After the Supreme Court held the First Amendment no bar, Minnesota enforces a reporter's promise of source confidentiality by promissory estoppel.
steps.effect: Enforcing source confidentiality

steps.note: Under the Texas rule applied in this excerpt, reliance on the oral loan accommodation did not overcome the writing requirement.
steps.effect: Requiring a promise about writing
steps.context: The missing allegation was a promise to sign a writing satisfying the statute. The assigned Tolosa source is an excerpt; a complete opinion and exact decision date remain unverified.

steps.note: Pennsylvania enforced this prosecutor’s nonprosecution assurance after reliance that surrendered protection against self-incrimination.
steps.effect: Enforcing due-process protection
steps.context: This is a due-process ruling in a criminal case, not a decision applying the ordinary civil-contract test in Restatement § 90.

timelines.guide: Compare an unenforced gift in Kirksey with the induced reliance in Ricketts and Feinberg. Drennan concerns keeping an offer open; Hoffman concerns negotiations. The later cases test remedies and other legal limits. Cosby belongs to a separate due-process branch.

timelines.title: Keeping an offer open
timelines.question: When can an offer no longer be withdrawn before acceptance?
timelines.anchor: when an offer cannot be revoked
timelines.now: An offer can become irrevocable through an option bargain, invited performance, an applicable statute, or protected reliance. Each route has conditions. Model UCC § 2-205 protects a merchant’s signed goods offer without consideration for no more than three months; an assurance on the recipient’s form needs a separate signature.

steps.note: A promise to hold an offer open, given without consideration, does not bind; the offeror may revoke, and word from a third party is enough notice.
steps.effect: Allowing withdrawal without an option

steps.note: Beginning the invited performance can protect the opportunity to finish before the offer is withdrawn.
steps.effect: Protecting begun performance
steps.context: This rule concerns an offer inviting performance rather than a return promise. The offeror’s duty remains conditional on completion; merely preparing to perform presents a different issue.

steps.note: Learned Hand: a supplier's bid used in a contractor's bid stays revocable, and promissory estoppel does not hold an offer that sought a bargain.
steps.fate: Drennan takes a contrary approach in California (1958); § 87(2) later states the reliance approach. Neither overrules this Second Circuit decision.
steps.effect: Rejecting reliance on this bid

steps.note: New York: a signed written offer that states it is irrevocable binds for the stated period, or a reasonable time, without consideration.
steps.effect: Protecting signed New York offers

steps.note: Model UCC § 2-205 can hold a merchant’s signed goods offer open without consideration, for at most three months.
steps.effect: Protecting merchants’ signed offers
steps.context: The writing must assure that the offer will be held open. Protection lasts for the stated time or a reasonable time, subject to that cap; an assurance on the recipient’s form needs a separate signature.

steps.note: Reasonable, foreseeable reliance on the bid protected a reasonable opportunity to accept after the general award.
steps.effect: Protecting reasonable bid reliance
steps.context: A contractor cannot rely on a bid it knows or should know is mistaken, or keep the offer open while shopping for a better deal.

steps.note: The Second Restatement follows Drennan’s reliance rationale: foreseeable substantial reliance before acceptance can bind an offer as an option to the extent necessary to avoid injustice, not automatically for every use of a bid.
steps.effect: Stating reliance-based option protection

timelines.guide: Dickinson begins with an unsupported promise to keep an offer open. Then compare invited performance, a signed statutory assurance, and reliance. Baird and Drennan reach different results in different courts; neither is an appeal from the other.

timelines.title: Offer and acceptance: communicating agreement
timelines.question: Which words or actions create an offer or accept one?
timelines.anchor: what words and acts count as offer and acceptance
timelines.now: Assent depends on outward words and conduct in context. An offer invites commitment; acceptance makes that commitment in an allowed manner. Goods offers generally permit any reasonable method unless the offer clearly indicates otherwise. Whether performance needs separate notice depends on the offer and whether the offeror would learn of it.

steps.note: Acceptance needs an outward act put in the course of communication to the offeror; private preparations to perform are not enough (New York).
steps.effect: Rejecting private preparations

steps.note: Objective legal commitment depends on context. This English domestic support arrangement did not establish the contract alleged; ordinary family arrangements are not automatically enforceable bargains.
steps.effect: Reading family promises in context

steps.note: The offeror controls the manner: an order that makes home-office approval the acceptance needs no separate notice of that approval (Texas).
steps.effect: Accepting by specified approval

steps.note: Unless the offer clearly says otherwise, acceptance may be made in any reasonable manner, including a prompt promise to ship or prompt shipment.
steps.effect: Allowing reasonable acceptance methods

steps.note: Assent is read from outward words and acts as a reasonable person would take them; a secret intent to joke does not undo a signed sale (Virginia).
steps.effect: Enforcing outward agreement

steps.note: An advertisement that is clear, definite and leaves nothing open is an offer; the store cannot add a 'women only' rule after acceptance (Minnesota).
steps.effect: Treating a definite ad as an offer

steps.note: This response did not definitely commit to the land-sale offer, so it was not an acceptance.
steps.effect: Requiring a definite commitment
steps.context: The court assessed the particular words expressing readiness while requesting information. The lesson is to examine whether the response commits—not to treat every question accompanying acceptance as a rejection.

timelines.guide: Ask what a reasonable recipient would understand, then check the acceptance method the offer invites. Compare private preparations, company approval, a signed land sale and a definite advertisement. These settings test different parts of formation.

timelines.title: Conflicting forms: formation and contract terms
timelines.question: If the buyer’s and seller’s forms differ, is there a contract—and which terms belong to it?
timelines.anchor: how far an acceptance may vary the offer and still form a contract
timelines.now: Model UCC § 2-207 can recognize a contract even when the forms differ. Expressly conditional acceptance, additional terms between merchants, and a contract formed through conduct require separate analysis. Northrop predicts Illinois’s approach to conflicting terms; that prediction is not a uniform rule for every state.

steps.note: The buyer’s changed-quantity response rejected the offer; the buyer could not later revive it by accepting alone.
steps.effect: Rejecting a changed-quantity acceptance
steps.context: The opinion expressly allows the original offeror to renew the offer or agree to the change. It does not say the parties can never revive negotiations.

steps.note: For sales of goods the Code drops the mirror-image rule: an acceptance can form a contract though it adds or changes terms.
steps.effect: Allowing agreement despite different forms

steps.note: An acceptance is expressly conditional only if it clearly says the offeree will not proceed without assent to its terms; 'subject to' is not enough.
steps.effect: Testing conditional acceptance

steps.note: When forms do not form a contract but both sides perform, § 2-207(3) supplies the terms the writings share plus Code gap-fillers.
steps.effect: Finding a contract through conduct

steps.note: Different terms in offer and acceptance knock each other out and Code gap-fillers replace them: the majority rule, predicted for Illinois.
steps.effect: Canceling conflicting warranty terms

steps.note: Between merchants, an additional term may enter the contract; the party opposing it had to prove material alteration.
steps.effect: Testing an additional merchant term
steps.context: Section 2-207(2) excludes an additional term if the offer limits acceptance, the term materially alters the bargain, or a timely objection occurs. Bayway addressed the material-alteration branch.

timelines.guide: Keep three questions separate: do the writings form a contract, which added or conflicting terms enter, and did conduct create a contract despite the writings? Dorton addresses conditional acceptance; C. Itoh addresses conduct; Northrop and Bayway address different kinds of terms.

timelines.title: Standard terms: notice and agreement
timelines.question: When can unread printed or online terms bind someone?
timelines.anchor: when standard terms bind without real bargaining
timelines.now: Unread terms can bind if the governing law recognizes adequate notice and assent. Keeping goods, clicking a button and continuing to use a service are not interchangeable acts. Fairness, federal arbitration law and the timing of amendments may pose additional questions even after formation.

steps.note: A liability limit printed on a claim check binds only with reasonable notice and assent; taking the ticket is not assent as a matter of law (New York).
steps.effect: Requiring notice beyond a claim ticket

steps.note: A non-negotiated forum clause in a form ticket is enforceable if reasonable and fundamentally fair; notice of the clause was conceded.
steps.effect: Enforcing a fair forum clause

steps.note: The Seventh Circuit treated keeping the computer beyond the return period as acceptance of its boxed terms.
steps.effect: Accepting boxed terms by retention
steps.context: Hill followed ProCD’s formation approach. Compare Klocek’s different account of who made the offer; the cases do not establish one uniform rule for every term shipped with goods.

steps.note: This court treated the buyer as the offeror and the boxed terms as proposed additions.
steps.effect: Treating boxed terms as proposals
steps.context: Under its § 2-207 analysis, a consumer’s retention of the computer did not itself expressly accept the additional terms. Compare Hill’s different formation approach.

steps.note: Online terms bind only if the screen reasonably shows they exist and that clicking means assent; terms hidden below a download button did not.
steps.effect: Rejecting hidden download terms

steps.note: The FAA preempted California’s rule requiring classwide procedures as a condition of enforcing this arbitration agreement.
steps.effect: Preempting a class-arbitration condition
steps.context: The decision did not validate every standard term or eliminate generally applicable contract defenses.

steps.note: Inquiry notice suffices: a clear sign-up screen linking the terms binds a user who registers, without an 'I agree' box (California law).
steps.effect: Finding notice on the signup screen

steps.note: The district court refused to apply the arbitration amendment to the remaining pre-amendment claims.
steps.effect: Rejecting an arbitration amendment
steps.context: Website posting and continued use did not supply adequate notice on this record. A separate retroactivity analysis also excluded these claims; the later claims had been dismissed by stipulation.

timelines.guide: First separate notice from agreement, then ask whether another rule limits enforcement. Hill and Klocek analyze boxed terms differently. Specht and Meyer focus on screen design. Anderson concerns adding arbitration to an existing relationship.

timelines.title: Open terms and unfinished negotiations
timelines.question: What can be enforceable before every term is settled?
timelines.anchor: when an unfinished bargain or failed negotiation creates liability
timelines.now: For goods, open terms do not defeat a contract if the parties intended to be bound and a sufficiently certain remedy exists. A promise to negotiate or a reliance claim can create a different obligation. Neither route automatically supplies the final deal the parties never made. The French statute is a separate comparison.

steps.note: Leaving the price and how long it would run for later agreement makes an unenforceable agreement to agree; the court will not supply them (New York).
steps.fate: Later model UCC §§ 2-204 and 2-305 permit some intended goods contracts despite open terms. They do not automatically enforce every unfinished bargain: § 2-305(4) preserves the parties’ choice not to be bound until price is agreed.
steps.effect: Rejecting unresolved pricing terms

steps.note: A sale of goods does not fail for open terms if the parties meant to contract and there is a reasonably certain basis for a remedy.
steps.effect: Allowing intended contracts with open terms

steps.note: Reliance in negotiations: Wisconsin awards reliance losses on promises made during franchise talks that were too indefinite for a contract.
steps.effect: Protecting negotiation reliance

steps.note: A letter of intent with an express promise to negotiate in good faith can itself be an enforceable contract (Pennsylvania law predicted).
steps.effect: Recognizing a negotiation commitment

steps.note: When parties meant to stay bound and their pricing mechanism fails, a court may set a reasonable price and supervise continued performance (Ohio).
steps.effect: Replacing a failed pricing mechanism

steps.note: New York promissory estoppel yields reliance damages, including attributable overhead, when talks never produced the contemplated contract.
steps.effect: Compensating reliance expenditures

steps.note: The alleged promise to consider a loan modification supported allowing the reliance claim to proceed.
steps.effect: Allowing a modification-reliance claim
steps.context: The federal court predicted Massachusetts law. Surviving dismissal did not establish liability or prove that the parties had agreed to a final modification.

steps.note: France codifies good faith in negotiations: fault in negotiating yields damages, but never the benefits expected from the unmade contract.
steps.effect: Regulating negotiations in France

timelines.guide: Distinguish a final agreement with an open term from a promise to negotiate and from reliance on a negotiation promise. Sun Printing and Oglebay concern missing pricing terms; Channel Home concerns a negotiation commitment; Hoffman and Cyberchron concern reliance.

timelines.title: Changing a contract: consideration and pressure
timelines.question: When is a promise to change an existing contract enforceable?
timelines.anchor: the pre-existing duty rule
timelines.now: A services modification may encounter the pre-existing-duty rule. Model UCC § 2-209 removes consideration as a requirement for a goods modification, but the modification must meet the Code’s test of good faith. New York’s statute for a writing signed by the party against whom the change is enforced and the Restatement’s fair-modification approach offer distinct routes. None makes coercion irrelevant.

steps.note: The court refused the promised raise because the fishermen offered only work they already owed.
steps.fate: Section 2-209 supplies a different rule for goods contracts; it does not change this services holding.
steps.effect: Rejecting extra pay for existing duties
steps.context: This was the traditional pre-existing-duty analysis of a services contract. The separate goods-modification rule does not change this holding.

steps.note: New York: a written agreement to modify or discharge a contract, signed by the party against whom it is to be enforced or by that party's agent, does not fail for lack of consideration.
steps.effect: Recognizing signed modifications

steps.note: Parties may rescind and replace a deal in one transaction; an owner who freely gives up the old price after unforeseen rock and promises a fair special rate is bound to it (New Hampshire).
steps.effect: Enforcing a voluntary price adjustment

steps.note: An agreement modifying a sales contract needs no consideration; the Code's comments police modifications by a test of good faith instead.
steps.effect: Dispensing with new consideration

steps.note: The threatened supply cutoff left no timely substitute or adequate breach remedy, making the modification voidable for duress.
steps.effect: Rejecting a coerced modification
steps.context: Duress is separate from consideration: satisfying the consideration requirement does not validate a coerced modification.

timelines.guide: Ask two questions: does the change satisfy the applicable consideration or substitute rule, and was the agreement validly obtained? Alaska Packers addresses existing duties; Watkins addresses a voluntary adjustment; Austin addresses economic duress.

timelines.title: Unconscionability: unfair terms and unfair bargaining
timelines.question: When may a court refuse to enforce an oppressive bargain?
timelines.anchor: when a court may refuse to enforce a term as unconscionable
timelines.now: Unconscionability examines the bargain when it was made. Lack of meaningful choice and seriously one-sided terms are central concerns, but jurisdictions differ in their tests and balance. Arbitration agreements remain subject to general contract defenses within federal preemption limits.

steps.note: The Code lets a court refuse to enforce a contract or clause it finds unconscionable when made, without defining the term.
steps.effect: Authorizing refusal of oppressive terms

steps.note: The court recognized a test combining lack of meaningful choice with unreasonably one-sided terms.
steps.effect: Examining choice and one-sidedness
steps.context: It sent the case back to apply that test. It did not itself decide that the challenged contracts were unconscionable.

steps.note: California: adhesion terms bind unless outside reasonable expectations or unduly oppressive; one side's own ally cannot be sole arbitrator.
steps.effect: Rejecting a biased arbitration setup

steps.note: California applies a sliding scale of procedural and substantive unconscionability and refuses a one-sided mandatory employment arbitration agreement.
steps.effect: Testing employment arbitration fairness

steps.note: Oklahoma applies the two-part test: a hidden, one-sided litter clause the buyers could not understand is unconscionable as a matter of law.
steps.effect: Rejecting the chicken-litter clause

steps.note: The FAA preempts a state rule, framed as unconscionability, that conditions arbitration agreements on the availability of class procedures.
steps.effect: Preempting a class-arbitration condition

steps.note: After Concepcion, unconscionability remains a general defense to arbitration, and several one-sided terms can defeat the whole agreement (California).
steps.effect: Applying ordinary contract defenses

timelines.guide: Look at both the bargaining process and the substance of the terms. The cases explain those inquiries in different jurisdictions. Concepcion adds a federal arbitration limit; Samaniego shows that ordinary contract defenses still require analysis.

timelines.title: Written contracts and outside evidence
timelines.question: Can outside evidence add a term, correct a mistake, or explain the writing?
timelines.anchor: how much evidence outside the writing a court will hear
timelines.now: A court first identifies the problem: completeness, interpretation or correction of a mistake. Different rules govern each. California permits preliminary consideration of evidence about meaning; New York and Pennsylvania apply their own limits. The CISG follows a separate framework for international sales.

steps.note: Where the writing is complete on a subject, an oral term the parties would naturally have put in it is barred, even as a separate deal (Pennsylvania).
steps.effect: Excluding an omitted sales promise

steps.note: New York: a prior oral term is provable only if collateral in form, consistent with the writing, and not one the parties would ordinarily put in it.
steps.effect: Testing a collateral oral agreement

steps.note: The buyer failed to prove that the agreed word “chicken” had the narrower meaning it claimed.
steps.effect: Deciding what “chicken” meant
steps.context: The court considered negotiations, trade evidence and regulatory usage. This concerns interpretation of the agreed description, not a freestanding exception to the parol evidence rule.

steps.note: The rule does not bar reformation: a term left out by mutual mistake may be proved and written back in (Pennsylvania).
steps.effect: Correcting a mistakenly omitted term

steps.note: California admits a collateral oral term the parties might naturally have made separately, unless the writing was meant as the whole bargain.
steps.effect: Considering a separate oral term

steps.note: Extrinsic evidence is admissible whenever relevant to a meaning the words are reasonably susceptible to, however plain the writing looks (California).
steps.effect: Considering evidence of intended meaning

steps.note: Trade usage and course of performance can supplement the written price term when reasonably consistent with it. The Hawaii asphalt-market evidence supported price protection in this transaction.
steps.effect: Recognizing trade-based price protection

steps.note: California law required a chance to offer outside evidence despite apparently clear loan documents.
steps.effect: Allowing evidence without deciding meaning
steps.context: The Ninth Circuit criticized but applied that rule. Footnote 6 still allowed later summary judgment unless the evidence made the writing reasonably susceptible to Trident’s proposed meaning.

steps.note: New York would not use outside evidence to create ambiguity in this complete, clear written agreement.
steps.effect: Enforcing a clear integrated writing
steps.context: This is a contrasting jurisdictional approach, not a later overruling of California’s interpretation cases.

steps.note: New York again reads the writing on its face: silence about a use does not make a clear, unconditional transfer of ownership ambiguous.
steps.effect: Reading an unrestricted ownership transfer

steps.note: Under the CISG, which has no parol evidence rule, a merger clause binds only if both parties meant it to; negotiations count under Article 8.
steps.effect: Considering negotiations under the CISG

timelines.guide: These are three different questions. Gianni and Masterson address omitted terms; Bollinger addresses correcting a mistaken writing; Pacific Gas and Trident address meaning. Compare the California approach with New York’s stricter treatment of clear writings.

timelines.title: Contract meaning in business practice
timelines.question: How do industry customs and the parties’ behavior affect a written deal?
timelines.anchor: how far usage and dealing may shape the written terms
timelines.now: Under the UCC, business context can explain or supplement a writing without first finding its words ambiguous. Express terms generally control an irreconcilable conflict, while performance may also show waiver or modification. A claimed trade practice must be proved and must be applicable to the party charged with it.

steps.note: Trade usage may give seemingly plain words or figures a special trade meaning, with no prior finding of ambiguity (Oregon).
steps.effect: Reading numbers through trade practice

steps.note: The UCC makes trade practice and the parties’ conduct part of the interpretation inquiry.
steps.effect: Recognizing business context
steps.context: The 1952 provisions were §§ 1-205 and 2-202. Revised § 1-303 brings the context rules together: express terms generally prevail, but performance can show waiver or modification under §§ 1-303(f) and 2-209.

steps.note: The party claiming the narrower meaning of an ambiguous term must prove it, and a usage binds a newcomer only if known or so general as to be presumed.
steps.effect: Requiring proof of a trade meaning

steps.note: Under the Code, usage and dealing come in without ambiguity unless irreconcilable with the express terms; a merger clause must expressly negate them.
steps.effect: Admitting usage and prior dealings

steps.note: Trade usage and course of performance can qualify an express posted-price term with price protection if reasonably consistent with it.
steps.effect: Qualifying price with trade practice

steps.note: Usage can cut the other way: an unrebutted trade usage supplied an exclusive repair-or-refund remedy as part of the agreement.
steps.effect: Finding a customary remedy limit

timelines.guide: Compare three kinds of context: industry practice, earlier dealings between these parties, and performance of this contract. Hurst and Frigaliment address the meaning of words; Nanakuli concerns price protection; Figgie concerns a remedy limit.

timelines.title: Misleading statements, silence and disclosures
timelines.question: When does misleading conduct undermine agreement?
timelines.anchor: when silence or loose talk is actionable
timelines.now: Whether silence or an opinion is actionable depends on the speaker’s duty, the context and the governing law. A partial statement can require further disclosure to avoid misleading the listener. Reliance is a separate issue: a specific disclaimer can defeat it under the law applied in Psenicska.

steps.note: A buyer need not disclose market news equally open to both sides, but neither party may say or do anything to mislead the other.
steps.effect: Distinguishing silence from misleading conduct

steps.note: The seller’s silence about a known hidden defect did not support this Massachusetts claim.
steps.fate: Johnson adopts a different Florida home-sale rule; it does not overrule this Massachusetts decision.
steps.effect: Applying Massachusetts caveat emptor
steps.context: The 1942 decision distinguished mere silence from a false statement, misleading half-truth or existing duty to speak. It is not a universal current rule permitting silence about home defects.

steps.note: The alleged expert praise could support a fraud claim despite taking the form of opinions.
steps.effect: Examining expert opinions for fraud
steps.context: Florida considered superior knowledge and the parties’ unequal ability to judge the subject. The decision permitted the allegations to proceed; it did not find that the fraud had been proved.

steps.note: Half-truths: one who speaks on a subject must disclose what is needed to keep the statement from misleading; Swinton is distinguished (Massachusetts).
steps.effect: Requiring an honest complete account

steps.note: Florida required a home seller to disclose known material facts that were not readily observable and were unknown to the buyer.
steps.effect: Requiring Florida home-sale disclosure
steps.context: The duty concerns facts materially affecting property value. The buyer’s lack of knowledge is part of the test; the earlier note omitted it.

steps.note: Aspirational sales talk is puffery, not fraud, and Illinois promissory fraud needs a scheme to defraud beyond one broken promise.
steps.effect: Distinguishing puffery from fraud

steps.note: The specific release defeated reasonable reliance under New York law as applied to these Borat claims.
steps.effect: Enforcing a specific reliance disclaimer
steps.context: The court considered a peculiar-knowledge exception but found it inapplicable on this record. A specific disclaimer is not an exceptionless answer to every fraud claim.

timelines.guide: Compare complete silence (Swinton) with a misleading partial account (Kannavos), expert praise (Vokes), and a specific disclaimer (Psenicska). Johnson’s Florida home-sale duty is a different jurisdiction’s rule, not an overruling of Swinton.

timelines.title: Conditions: when a duty becomes due
timelines.question: Must an event occur before the other party has to perform?
timelines.anchor: how strictly conditions are enforced
timelines.now: A condition makes a duty depend on an event. Courts may interpret language, recognize waiver or apply substantial-performance rules to prevent disproportionate loss. Those doctrines do not automatically replace an unmistakable express condition. The contract’s language and the governing law matter.

steps.note: Mansfield: the order of performance follows the parties' evident sense; giving security was a condition precedent to the sale of the business.
steps.effect: Requiring security before transfer

steps.note: An express condition of personal satisfaction is enforced: a buyer who reserved the right to reject a portrait he disliked need not pay (Michigan).
steps.effect: Honoring personal satisfaction

steps.note: Divisibility limits forfeiture: where the price is set per unit, the performer recovers for each unit fully delivered (Pennsylvania).
steps.effect: Paying for completed divisible units

steps.note: Waiver: an owner who kept paying without asking for the architect's certificates cannot invoke their absence against final payment (Pennsylvania).
steps.effect: Preventing forfeiture after waived certificates

steps.note: An innocent, trivial construction departure did not require forfeiting payment for substantially completed work.
steps.effect: Recognizing substantial performance
steps.context: Substantial performance applies to promises and constructive conditions in this setting. It does not generally substitute for strict compliance with an unmistakable express condition.

steps.note: After diligent efforts failed to obtain the specified mortgage, the buyers could recover their deposit.
steps.effect: Returning a deposit after financing fails
steps.context: The available loan exceeded the agreed interest ceiling. They did not have to accept the sellers’ proposed subsidy instead of the financing condition they had negotiated.

steps.note: An ambiguous pay-when-paid clause fixes a time for payment, not a condition; shifting the owner's credit risk needs clear words (Florida).
steps.effect: Reading payment language as timing

timelines.guide: First distinguish a condition from a promise about performance. Then ask whether the agreement is divisible, the condition was waived, or substantial performance applies. Compare those routes with Luttinger’s failed financing condition and Peacock’s ambiguous payment language.

timelines.title: Failed assumptions: later events and initial mistakes
timelines.question: Who bears the risk when the bargain’s assumptions fail?
timelines.anchor: when an unexpected event excuses performance
timelines.now: Impossibility and frustration address later events; mutual mistake addresses a mistaken assumption at formation. The contract and governing law allocate risk. Increased expense or a disappointing bargain alone did not establish an excuse in the cases here. Read the historical decisions as distinct applications, not one universal test.

steps.note: Where performance depends on a particular thing, its destruction without fault excuses both sides: the law implies a condition.
steps.effect: Excusing a destroyed performance venue

steps.note: A builder's absolute promise binds despite unforeseen soil; hardship short of impossibility is no excuse (Minnesota).
steps.fate: Compare United States v. Spearin (1918): when the government required compliance with its plans, it warranted their adequacy. That distinct allocation of design risk is not an overruling of Stees.
steps.effect: Enforcing the builder’s assumed risk

steps.note: Mistake at formation: a sale may be avoided when both parties erred about the substance of the thing, not merely its quality (Michigan).
steps.fate: Lenawee County v. Messerly (Michigan, 1982) limited Sherwood’s substance-versus-quality distinction to its facts and adopted a basic-assumption and risk-allocation analysis.
steps.effect: Examining a mistake about the bargain

steps.note: Frustration of purpose: when the shared foundation of the deal fails, the parties are discharged though performance is still possible.
steps.effect: Excusing a frustrated shared purpose

steps.note: California accepts frustration but confines it: the event must be unforeseeable and destroy nearly all the value of the return performance.
steps.effect: Rejecting this frustration defense

steps.note: Impracticability needs an unexpected event, a risk not allocated by agreement or custom, and real impracticability; extra cost alone did not suffice.
steps.effect: Finding a more costly voyage practicable

steps.note: Arizona rescinds for a mutual mistake about a basic assumption (Restatement (Second) § 152) but limits the buyer to restitution, not reliance costs.
steps.effect: Rescinding for a shared water mistake

timelines.guide: Put the problem on the right side of formation. Taylor, Krell and Transatlantic concern later events; Sherwood and Renner concern mistakes already present when the parties contracted. In either setting, ask who accepted the risk.

timelines.title: Fixing the work or paying the lost value
timelines.question: Should damages pay for completion or for the property’s reduced value?
timelines.anchor: what the owner recovers for defective or unfinished work
timelines.now: Completion cost and lost market value can produce very different awards. The cases weigh the promised purpose, proportionality, the character of the breach and waste. They do not establish that either deliberate breach or expensive repair dictates the same result in every jurisdiction.

steps.note: When replacing innocent defective work would cost far more than the value it adds, the measure is diminution in value (New York).
steps.effect: Using lost value for trivial deviation

steps.note: Minnesota awards the cost of the promised grading for a deliberate breach, though it far exceeds the value the work would add to the land.
steps.effect: Awarding the promised completion cost

steps.note: Repair cost for defects reasonably fixable; diminution in value where the fix would mean tearing out work, as with the misplaced wall (Wisconsin).
steps.effect: Separating repair cost from waste

steps.note: Oklahoma caps damages at diminution in value when the broken term was incidental and its cost grossly exceeds the value it would add.
steps.effect: Limiting incidental restoration damages

steps.note: England's middle course: rebuilding cost is out when unreasonable, but the owner may recover for loss of amenity rather than nothing.
steps.effect: Compensating lost enjoyment without rebuilding

timelines.guide: Compare what was promised, why it mattered, and the cost of correcting the failure. Groves and Peevyhouse reach contrasting results in different states. Ruxley adds an English example of compensation for lost enjoyment without rebuilding.

timelines.title: Which losses can damages cover?
timelines.question: Was the loss foreseeable, avoidable, and proved with enough certainty?
timelines.anchor: what losses a plaintiff can recover
timelines.now: Causation alone does not make every loss recoverable. Foreseeability, reasonable certainty and avoidability impose distinct limits. Apply each jurisdiction’s formulation: New York’s Kenford decisions, for example, ask about contemplated liability as well as the ability to estimate losses.

steps.note: Recoverable losses arise naturally from breach or were within both parties' contemplation when contracting; uncommunicated special losses are out.
steps.effect: Limiting recovery to contemplated losses

steps.note: Avoidable loss: after a clear repudiation the other party may not keep performing and charge the cost; recovery is costs to date plus profit.
steps.effect: Stopping avoidable post-repudiation costs

steps.note: Parker could reject the different and inferior substitute role without losing her guaranteed-pay recovery.
steps.effect: Rejecting a different inferior job
steps.context: California distinguished actual replacement earnings from hypothetical earnings from rejected work. To deduct the latter, the employer had to show comparable or substantially similar employment.

steps.note: Certainty: a new business is not barred from lost profits; a reasonable basis for estimating them suffices, though the jury may not guess (Michigan).
steps.effect: Allowing proof of new-business profits

steps.note: New York: twenty years of projected stadium profits are too speculative, and the county never contemplated liability for them.
steps.effect: Rejecting speculative stadium profits

steps.note: New York requires that liability for an unusual loss was contemplated at contracting, stricter than mere foreseeability, and denies land appreciation.
steps.effect: Rejecting uncontemplated land appreciation

timelines.guide: Use three separate checks. Hadley and Kenford ask which risks the contract covered; Rockingham and Parker concern losses that might have been avoided; Fera and the first Kenford decision concern proof of lost profits.

timelines.title: What is the remedy trying to restore?
timelines.question: Does recovery protect the promised bargain, reliance, or a benefit conferred?
timelines.anchor: what the injured party may recover
timelines.now: The remedy’s purpose determines what is measured. Hawkins protects a promised result; Sullivan addresses reliance-related losses; restitution cases measure retained benefits. Ordinary contract damages do not automatically transfer the breacher’s profits to the claimant. EarthInfo illustrates an exceptional disgorgement inquiry.

steps.note: Expectation: the value of the promised result minus the value of what was delivered; pain the operation would have caused anyway is not compensated.
steps.effect: Measuring the promised result

steps.note: Restitution for the party in breach: a builder short of substantial performance recovers the benefit conferred less the owner's damages (Idaho).
steps.effect: Paying a breaching builder’s net benefit

steps.note: Contract damages compensate: punitive damages are unavailable even for a malicious breach unless a tort is pleaded and proved (Wisconsin).
steps.effect: Refusing punishment for breach alone

steps.note: The broken surgical promise supported recovery for expenses, worsening, and additional pain and distress.
steps.effect: Compensating the broken surgical promise
steps.context: The court found these items recoverable under either a reliance or expectation measure; the ordinary pain the promised treatment would itself have entailed was a different issue.

steps.note: Restitution for the injured party: a subcontractor who quits after a material breach recovers the value conferred, not reduced by its losing bargain.
steps.fate: Restatement (Third) of Restitution § 38 (2011) proposes a contract-price limit. A Restatement does not itself overrule this Fourth Circuit holding.
steps.effect: Recovering value despite a losing bargain

steps.note: Ordinary contract damages measure the plaintiff's loss; the breacher's gains count only insofar as they track that loss.
steps.effect: Measuring the claimant’s own loss

steps.note: Colorado allows disgorgement for a conscious, substantial breach where damages are inadequate, less profits due to the breacher's own contribution.
steps.effect: Considering disgorgement for substantial breach

timelines.guide: Expectation asks where performance would have left the claimant. Reliance asks about losses incurred in reliance. Restitution asks what benefit the other side received. Keep a breaching party’s restitution claim separate from an injured party’s; disgorgement adds another question.

timelines.title: Ordering performance or stopping a breach
timelines.question: When is money an inadequate remedy?
timelines.anchor: when a court orders performance instead of damages
timelines.now: Specific performance and injunctions depend on the adequacy of damages and equitable judgment. Model UCC § 2-716 permits specific performance for unique goods or other proper circumstances. A higher replacement price alone does not make money inadequate. Orders involving personal services raise separate limits.

steps.note: Equity will not compel a singer to perform, but it will enjoin her breach of an express promise not to sing elsewhere during the engagement.
steps.effect: Restraining competing performances

steps.note: Model UCC § 2-716 permits specific performance for unique goods or other proper circumstances.
steps.effect: Allowing relief beyond unique goods
steps.context: Difficulty obtaining a substitute can matter even without a uniqueness label. The adequacy of damages and equitable discretion still require analysis.

steps.note: A horse trained by the buyer has unique value to him, so equity orders its delivery despite the usual rule for chattels (Arkansas).
steps.effect: Ordering delivery of a trained horse

steps.note: The used jet was not shown to be unique, and a higher replacement price did not make damages inadequate.
steps.effect: Finding damages adequate for a jet
steps.context: Specific performance under UCC § 2-716 therefore failed on this record.

steps.note: Posner: an injunction against breach of an exclusivity covenant is proper when damages are inadequate, judged by the costs and benefits of each remedy.
steps.effect: Protecting exclusivity with an injunction

timelines.guide: Compare an order delivering a particular good with an injunction stopping prohibited conduct. Morris concerns a specially trained horse; Klein concerns replacement aircraft; Walgreen concerns a hard-to-price exclusivity promise. Lumley distinguishes forbidding competing work from compelling service.

timelines.title: Agreed damages or an unenforceable penalty?
timelines.question: Will the court enforce the amount chosen for breach?
timelines.anchor: when a stipulated sum is enforced
timelines.now: The American cases test an agreed sum against reasonable compensation, using different jurisdictional formulations. New Jersey places the burden on the challenger in a bargain between commercial equals. The Swiss case instead concerns judicial reduction of an excessive penalty under that legal regime.

steps.note: A fixed sum is liquidated damages, not a penalty, if harm was hard to estimate at formation and the sum was a reasonable forecast (South Dakota).
steps.effect: Upholding estimated delay damages

steps.note: A formula paying full revenue without deducting the costs the promisee saves is a penalty; Posner questions the rule but applies it (Illinois law).
steps.effect: Rejecting a revenue-based penalty

steps.note: New Jersey tests reasonableness in all the circumstances and presumes a clause between commercial equals valid; the challenger bears the burden.
steps.effect: Testing reasonableness and proof

steps.note: The assigned translated Swiss decision permits judicial reduction of excessive contractual penalties. This comparative account does not establish the rule in an American jurisdiction.
steps.effect: Reducing an excessive Swiss penalty

timelines.guide: Ask whether the amount operates as reasonable compensation or punishment under the applicable law. Compare estimated delay loss in Gustafson, saved costs ignored in Lake River, and the challenged formula in Wasserman’s. Swiss penalty law supplies a separate comparison.

timelines.title: Enforcing a promise made for someone else
timelines.question: Was the outsider an intended beneficiary or merely someone who benefited?
timelines.anchor: who may sue on a contract made for their benefit
timelines.now: A benefit alone does not necessarily confer enforcement rights. The intended/incidental distinction asks what the contracting parties’ agreement was meant to accomplish. Government contracts require particular care. The cases and Restatement offer jurisdiction-dependent approaches, not a right for everyone helped by a contract.

steps.note: New York lets a creditor of the promisee sue the promisor on a promise made for his benefit, though he was no party and gave no consideration.
steps.effect: Allowing the intended creditor to sue

steps.note: Donee beneficiaries: a niece may enforce a promise made to her dying aunt for her benefit; closeness of kinship is not a strict limit (New York).
steps.effect: Enforcing a promised family benefit

steps.note: A city's water-supply contract benefits the public only incidentally; a resident may sue only if it promised compensation to individuals (New York).
steps.effect: Rejecting incidental public-benefit rights

steps.note: The Second Restatement replaces its creditor/donee terminology with intended and incidental beneficiaries, conditioned on the contracting parties’ intention. It proposes a framework; it does not enact a uniform state rule.
steps.effect: Distinguishing intended from incidental benefits

steps.note: South Dakota presumes against private enforcement of government contracts; an inmate is incidental to the State's food-service contract.
steps.effect: Rejecting rights under the service contract

steps.note: The same day: a settlement that expressly covers every Jewish inmate who asks for kosher meals is enforceable by a member of that class.
steps.effect: Recognizing rights under the settlement

timelines.guide: Lawrence involves a creditor; Seaver involves a promised gift. The Restatement reorganizes beneficiary categories. Compare the two Sisney cases to see why a general food-service agreement and an express settlement protecting a defined group produce different answers.

timelines.title: Specific jurisdiction: connections to this lawsuit
timelines.question: When may a court hear a claim against a defendant from outside the forum?
timelines.anchor: how far a state may reach an absent defendant
timelines.now: For state-court specific jurisdiction, ask whether the defendant deliberately connected with the state, whether this claim arises out of or relates to those contacts, and whether jurisdiction is fair. Ford rejects a strict causation requirement on its facts. The divided product-distribution cases leave boundaries unsettled. Fuld concerns a separate federal Fifth Amendment setting.

steps.note: Pennoyer used territorial rules to reject a personal judgment against an absent nonresident who had not been personally served or appeared. Later cases replace that framework for absent defendants.
steps.fate: Its territorial test for absent defendants gave way to Shoe (1945)
steps.effect: Territory limits absent-defendant jurisdiction
steps.context: Power runs with territory: a personal judgment needs in-state service or a voluntary appearance, so an absent nonresident is out of reach.

steps.note: A company can face suit without being physically present when its connections to the state make this claim consistent with fair play and substantial justice.
steps.effect: Minimum contacts replace territorial presence
steps.context: Minimum contacts replace physical presence: suit is allowed if it does not offend traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice.

steps.note: A single contract with a substantial connection to the forum supports a suit on that contract.
steps.effect: One forum-linked contract can suffice

steps.note: The defendant must deliberately create a connection with the state. Another person’s decision to move there cannot create that connection for the defendant.
steps.effect: Defendant must create the forum connection
steps.context: Purposeful availment: the defendant must itself reach into the forum; the unilateral acts of others do not count.

steps.note: Stream of commerce in a state court: a component maker can be sued where its product, sold through ordinary distribution, causes injury.
steps.effect: Illinois accepts a product-distribution connection

steps.note: Acquiescing in a child's move to the forum is not purposeful availment, so the parent cannot be sued there for support.
steps.effect: Child’s move does not establish parental contacts

steps.note: Foreseeable travel of a product is not enough; the defendant's own conduct must make suit there foreseeable, as when it serves that market.
steps.effect: Product travel alone is insufficient

steps.note: Regular, substantial circulation in the forum supported jurisdiction over the libel claim despite the plaintiff’s limited forum ties; the jurisdictional inquiry concerns the defendant’s forum conduct.
steps.effect: Magazine sales connect the libel claim

steps.note: The intentional tort was expressly aimed at California, where the story and injury were centered. The effects analysis depends on defendant-created forum connections.
steps.effect: California-targeted libel supports jurisdiction

steps.note: A sustained franchise relationship directed toward the Florida headquarters supported jurisdiction even though the Michigan franchisee had not physically entered Florida.
steps.effect: Franchise relationship supports purposeful contacts
steps.context: Two steps, contacts then fairness: a long-term franchise deal aimed at a forum company is a contact even without physical entry.

steps.note: The remaining dispute between foreign manufacturers failed the fairness inquiry. The Justices did not agree on one test for contacts created through product distribution.
steps.effect: Foreign indemnity suit fails fairness review
steps.context: Eight Justices agree the remaining foreign indemnity suit is unreasonable. No majority chooses between awareness and additional forum-directed conduct as the stream-of-commerce contact test.

steps.note: One machine sale in New Jersey did not establish jurisdiction here. Six Justices agreed on the result, but no five agreed on a general test.
steps.effect: Isolated sale fails; rationale divided
steps.context: Six Justices reject jurisdiction, with no five-Justice rationale: four require state targeting; two concur on the isolated-sale record and decline a broader rule. The three dissenters take a broader market approach.

steps.note: The defendant’s own contacts must connect him to the forum itself; knowledge of the plaintiffs’ forum connections and foreseeable injury there did not supply those contacts.
steps.effect: Plaintiff’s residence is not defendant’s contact

steps.note: Relatedness is claim by claim: nonresidents' claims need their own link to the forum, and the sliding-scale approach is rejected.
steps.effect: Each claim needs a forum connection

steps.note: 'Arise out of or relate to' needs no strict causation: a maker that cultivates a market for a model can be sued where it injures.
steps.effect: Related claims need no strict causal link

steps.note: The Court upheld this targeted federal terrorism statute under the Fifth Amendment. It did not simply extend the state-court minimum-contacts test to federal jurisdiction.
steps.effect: Federal statute survives a distinct Fifth Amendment test
steps.context: A separate federal-statute branch: the Fifth Amendment does not import the Fourteenth Amendment’s minimum-contacts test. This targeted terrorism statute is valid; the Court leaves the outer limits and a separate reasonableness requirement open.

timelines.guide: Start with the defendant’s connection to the state, then ask how this lawsuit relates to that connection and whether hearing it there is fair. The line moves from territorial rules to those three questions. The divided product-distribution cases leave some boundaries unsettled; Fuld addresses a separate federal constitutional rule.

timelines.title: Targeted conduct: libel, torts and websites
timelines.question: When does conduct aimed at a forum, in print or online, support jurisdiction there?
timelines.anchor: when conduct aimed at the forum supports suit there
timelines.now: Look for the defendant’s own connection between the disputed conduct and the state. The plaintiff’s residence or injury there does not alone establish jurisdiction. For online conduct, a widely accessible or interactive website is not by itself the answer; the claim-related forum connection still matters.

steps.note: Regular magazine sales in a state support a libel suit there, even for nationwide damages and though the plaintiff has no ties to it.
steps.effect: Regular sales support the libel suit

steps.note: Effects test: individuals whose alleged intentional tort was aimed at the forum, knowing the harm would be felt there, can be sued there.
steps.effect: Expressly aimed conduct supplies forum connections

steps.note: This district court compared active online business with passive websites. Its sliding scale is a lower-court framework, not a national rule that website interactivity alone establishes jurisdiction.
steps.effect: District court compares online business activity
steps.context: A sliding scale for websites: knowing online business with forum residents supports jurisdiction; a passive site does not.

steps.note: The defendant's own conduct must connect him to the forum itself; an injury the plaintiff feels there is not enough, even for torts.
steps.effect: Injury location alone does not suffice

steps.note: After Walden, a website's reach and interactivity in a state do not support a libel suit unless the story or site was aimed there.
steps.effect: Fifth Circuit requires forum-directed libel conduct

timelines.guide: An injury felt in a state does not automatically let its courts hear the case. Follow what the defendant did to connect the disputed conduct to that state. The Internet cases apply this question to websites; Zippo is one district court’s approach, not a Supreme Court test.

timelines.title: General jurisdiction: where a company is at home
timelines.question: Where can a defendant be sued on any claim, even one unrelated to the forum?
timelines.anchor: when a defendant may be sued on any claim
timelines.now: A corporation is ordinarily subject to unrelated claims where it is incorporated or has its principal place of business, with exceptional cases such as Perkins. Doing substantial business elsewhere is usually insufficient. Consent is a separate route; Mallory resolved the due-process challenge to Pennsylvania’s express registration statute, not its Commerce Clause challenge.

steps.note: Shoe described earlier cases allowing unrelated claims after exceptionally substantial corporate activity. Its own dispute involved obligations arising from the company’s Washington activities.
steps.effect: Historical discussion of unrelated claims
steps.context: This is a starting point for the later general-jurisdiction cases, not the modern test by itself. Shoe warned that the nature of the activity mattered, not a mechanical count of contacts.

steps.note: A foreign company run from an Ohio office during wartime may be sued there on unrelated claims; due process permits it.
steps.effect: Wartime headquarters supports general jurisdiction

steps.note: Purchases, training trips and a single negotiating visit are not the continuous and systematic contacts needed for unrelated claims.
steps.effect: Purchases and training trips are insufficient

steps.note: Products reaching the state through distribution did not make these foreign corporations at home there. General jurisdiction needs more than this kind of local sales connection.
steps.effect: Corporation must be essentially at home
steps.context: General jurisdiction only where the corporation is essentially at home; products reaching the state through commerce do not count.

steps.note: A corporation is ordinarily at home where it is incorporated and headquartered. Extensive business in another state usually does not permit suits there on unrelated claims.
steps.effect: Large sales do not make every state home
steps.context: 'At home' means place of incorporation and principal place of business, save an exceptional case; heavy in-state business is not enough.

steps.note: A railroad with extensive in-state track and workers is still not at home there, and FELA's venue clause confers no jurisdiction.
steps.effect: Railroad’s local operations are insufficient

steps.note: Pennsylvania registration under an express consent statute satisfies the Due Process Clause under Pennsylvania Fire. This is separate from “at home” contacts; the Commerce Clause challenge was left for remand.
steps.effect: Express registration consent survives due-process challenge

timelines.guide: General jurisdiction lets a court hear claims unrelated to the company’s local activity. Follow the shift from descriptions of substantial business to the narrower “at home” test. Registration-based consent is a separate route; Mallory did not resolve every constitutional objection to it.

timelines.title: Personal jurisdiction: service, domicile, property and consent
timelines.question: Which traditional bases of jurisdiction survive the minimum-contacts test?
timelines.anchor: the traditional bases of jurisdiction without contacts
timelines.now: Domicile, valid consent and personal service on an individual voluntarily present in the state remain distinct routes. Property alone is no shortcut around minimum contacts. Check service separately: an agent must qualify under the governing rule, and Burnham’s result did not produce a single majority rationale.

steps.note: Jurisdiction rests on in-state service, voluntary appearance, or local property seized at the outset; consent and status cases are reserved.
steps.effect: Territorial service and property framework

steps.note: Under the historical rule, serving a visiting debtor allowed attachment of the debt owed to an absent creditor. Shaffer later rejects this property-based shortcut.
steps.fate: Overruled by Shaffer (1977)
steps.effect: Historical debt-attachment route
steps.context: A debt follows the debtor: serving him on a brief visit lets the state seize what he owes an absent creditor.

steps.note: Implied consent: driving on a state's roads appoints a state official to receive service in suits about the driving, with notice to the driver.
steps.effect: Highway use supports statutory service consent

steps.note: Presence obtained by fraud does not count: a defendant lured into the state and served can attack the judgment where it is enforced.
steps.effect: Fraudulently induced presence defeats service

steps.note: A person’s domicile—their legal home—supports jurisdiction even while they are away, if they receive constitutionally adequate notice.
steps.effect: Domicile supports jurisdiction over an absentee
steps.context: Domicile suffices for a personal judgment against an absent resident given proper notice; 'fair play and substantial justice' starts here.

steps.note: Trickery by the party's lawyer that brings a nonresident into the state to be served also voids the service.
steps.effect: Lawyer’s trickery invalidates service

steps.note: The contract-appointed agent promptly forwarded the lawsuit papers, making service valid under the Federal Rule. The Court did not decide every due-process question about contractual consent.
steps.effect: Appointed agent’s prompt forwarding suffices
steps.context: The appointed process agent’s actual prompt forwarding validates service under the Federal Rule despite no advance promise to forward. The Court reserves failed notice and decides no due-process question; it does not approve every boilerplate forum term.

steps.note: Property alone no longer suffices: every assertion of jurisdiction, in rem or quasi in rem, must meet the Shoe standard.
steps.effect: Property must satisfy minimum-contacts analysis

steps.note: Personal jurisdiction is a waivable individual right, so a discovery sanction may establish the facts that support it.
steps.effect: Jurisdictional discovery sanctions can establish facts

steps.note: Tag jurisdiction survives Shaffer: personal service on a visitor inside the state is enough, though no rationale won a majority.
steps.effect: In-state personal service on visitor upheld

steps.note: Pennsylvania registration under an express consent statute satisfies the Due Process Clause under Pennsylvania Fire. This is separate from “at home” contacts; the Commerce Clause challenge was left for remand.
steps.effect: Express registration consent survives due-process challenge

timelines.guide: These are different routes to a court’s power over a defendant. Domicile means a person’s legal home; “tag” means personal service while the individual is in the state. Property and consent raise separate questions. A ruling approving a method of service does not necessarily decide the constitutional limits of jurisdiction.

timelines.title: Taking property before judgment: notice and a hearing
timelines.question: What notice and hearing does due process require before property is seized pending suit?
timelines.anchor: what notice and hearing must precede a taking
timelines.now: Notice must be reasonably calculated to reach those affected (Mullane). Whether a prejudgment seizure needs a prior hearing turns on the Mathews balance as Doehr adapted it: the owner's interest, the risk of error and the value of safeguards such as a judge, a bond and a prompt hearing, and the creditor's interest.

steps.note: Notice must be reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances, to inform interested parties and let them be heard.
steps.effect: Notice must reasonably reach affected people

steps.note: Freezing a worker's wages before judgment without notice and a prior hearing violates due process, even though it is temporary.
steps.effect: Wage freeze fails procedural safeguards

steps.note: A hearing comes before the state helps seize household goods, even briefly and with title disputed, save extraordinary situations.
steps.fate: Narrowed by Mitchell v. W. T. Grant (1974)
steps.effect: Household-goods seizure requires prior opportunity

steps.note: Louisiana’s procedure was upheld because a lien creditor supplied sworn facts to a judge, posted security and faced an immediate hearing on the debtor’s challenge.
steps.effect: Lien and procedural safeguards justify sequestration
steps.context: Mitchell sustains Louisiana sequestration for a lien creditor on sworn facts before a judge, with a creditor bond and an immediate debtor hearing. These safeguards qualify Fuentes; not every judge-issued seizure is valid.

steps.note: Garnishment issued by a clerk on a conclusory affidavit, with no judge and no early hearing, still violates due process.
steps.effect: Clerk-issued garnishment lacks adequate safeguards

steps.note: The process due is set by balancing the private interest, the risk of error and value of safeguards, and the government's interest.
steps.effect: Three interests determine the required process

steps.note: Mathews adapted for private remedies: attaching a home ex parte without exigency fails; the creditor's interest takes the state's place.
steps.effect: Home attachment fails the adapted balance

timelines.guide: A creditor may seek to freeze wages, goods or land before winning the lawsuit. Ask whether the owner gets notice and a meaningful chance to object soon enough. Compare the safeguards in each procedure; the cases do not announce that every seizure must use exactly the same process.

timelines.title: Erie: choosing between state and federal law
timelines.question: When a federal court hears a state-law claim, which questions must it decide under state law?
timelines.anchor: the reach of state law in federal court
timelines.now: Where no Federal Rule or statute covers the issue, a federal court applies the state rule if disregarding it would encourage forum shopping or produce inequitable administration of the laws (Hanna's twin aims), giving weight to strong federal interests such as the jury's role (Byrd) and accommodating both systems where it can (Gasperini).

steps.note: Federal courts decide questions of general commercial law for themselves; state decisions are respected but not binding.
steps.fate: Overruled by Erie (1938)
steps.effect: Federal courts choose general commercial law

steps.note: Swift at its height: a company reincorporates to create diversity and escape a state rule, and the federal court lets it.
steps.fate: Its premise fell with Swift in Erie (1938)
steps.effect: Reincorporation exposes Swift’s forum-shopping problem

steps.note: There is no federal general common law: in diversity cases state law, including state court decisions, supplies the rule of decision.
steps.effect: State law replaces general federal common law

steps.note: The federal court had to honor the state’s time limit for filing suit. Ignoring it would let a plaintiff win in federal court when the claim was time-barred in state court.
steps.fate: Confined by Hanna (1965) to Erie's twin aims
steps.effect: State limitations bar applies
steps.context: Outcome determination: a state limitations bar applies because ignoring it would change the result of the suit.

steps.note: A state rule that only service stops the limitations clock governs a diversity suit, though Rule 3 dates commencement from filing.
steps.effect: State service rule controls limitations tolling

steps.note: A state statute closing its courts to an unqualified foreign corporation closes the federal court in that state too.
steps.effect: State courthouse restriction follows diversity claim

steps.note: A state law requiring security for expenses applies in a federal derivative suit; the Federal Rule then in force did not conflict.
steps.effect: State expense-security requirement applies

steps.note: A state practice did not automatically control who decided the disputed facts. The federal system’s interest in allocating work to juries also mattered.
steps.effect: Federal jury interest can outweigh state practice
steps.context: Outcome is not everything: a state practice not bound up with the right yields to strong federal interests such as the jury's role.

steps.note: The outcome test is read through Erie's twin aims, discouraging forum shopping and inequitable administration of the laws.
steps.effect: Forum-shopping and unequal-treatment concerns guide analysis

steps.note: Reaffirms Ragan: Rule 3 governs commencement for federal procedural purposes, while the integral state service rule determines limitations tolling. There is no direct collision.
steps.effect: No conflict between Rule 3 and state tolling

steps.note: Accommodation: a state limit on excessive verdicts applies, enforced by the federal trial judge and reviewed for abuse of discretion.
steps.effect: State damages standard uses federal review structure

timelines.guide: A federal court can hear a state-law claim, but that does not let it invent the governing state law. First ask whether a valid federal statute or Federal Rule answers the disputed question. This timeline mainly follows what happens when neither does: state law, forum-shopping concerns and competing federal interests.

timelines.title: Erie: when a federal rule controls
timelines.question: When a Federal Rule or federal statute covers the question, does it displace state law in a diversity case?
timelines.anchor: when a Federal Rule or statute displaces state law
timelines.now: A valid Federal Rule governing the disputed question controls, subject to the Rules Enabling Act’s substantive-rights limitation and the Constitution. A federal statute must instead be constitutionally authorized. Walker finds no Rule collision; Shady Grove splits on validity, while Berk applies Rules 8 and 12 to Delaware’s affidavit requirement.

steps.note: The Rules Enabling Act lets the Supreme Court make procedural rules that do not abridge, enlarge or modify substantive rights.
steps.effect: Congress authorizes rules with substantive-rights limits

steps.note: A Rule is valid if it really regulates procedure; the importance of the interest it touches does not make it substantive.
steps.effect: Medical-examination rule regulates procedure

steps.note: Rule 3 does not determine when the state limitations period is tolled. The state service requirement applies; Walker later reaffirms this result after Hanna.
steps.effect: State service requirement controls tolling

steps.note: Rule 35 can require a defendant’s medical examination, but only when the particular condition is genuinely disputed and the requested examination has good cause.
steps.effect: Examinations require controversy and good cause
steps.context: Rule 35 can reach a defendant as well as a plaintiff, but requires a genuine controversy about the condition and good cause for the particular examination; procedural examination does not itself change substantive rights.

steps.note: A valid Federal Rule that covers the issue applies even if the outcome differs; Erie's twin-aims test does not decide Rules cases.
steps.effect: Valid Federal Rule governs the covered issue

steps.note: No direct collision: Rule 3 does not govern state tolling, so Ragan stands and state service law applies.
steps.effect: Rule 3 leaves state tolling untouched

steps.note: A federal rule broad enough to collide with state law controls: an appellate sanctions rule displaces a mandatory state penalty.
steps.effect: Federal appellate rule displaces state penalty

steps.note: The federal transfer statute governed the forum clause’s effect despite contrary state policy. Statutes and Federal Rules have different validity inquiries.
steps.effect: Federal transfer statute controls despite state policy
steps.context: A federal statute that covers the disputed issue controls if constitutionally valid. Section 1404(a) governs the forum clause’s effect on transfer despite contrary state policy; statutes do not undergo the separate Rules Enabling Act test for Federal Rules.

steps.note: Rule 41(b) does not prescribe the claim-preclusive effect of a diversity judgment. Federal common law ordinarily borrows the forum state’s preclusion law, subject to federal interests.
steps.effect: Rule 41 does not determine later preclusion

steps.note: Five Justices allowed this Rule 23 class action despite New York’s restriction. They divided over how to test a Federal Rule’s effect on substantive rights.
steps.effect: Class may proceed; validity rationale divided
steps.context: Five Justices let the Rule 23 class proceed despite New York’s penalty-class bar. No majority adopts one validity test: Scalia’s plurality reads procedure categorically; Stevens asks whether the state rule defines substantive rights.

steps.note: The majority held that federal pleading Rules 8 and 12 displaced Delaware’s affidavit requirement. Justice Jackson reached the same result through a different Rules analysis.
steps.effect: Federal pleading rules displace affidavit requirement
