reviewSources.label: Per curiam Parts II-A and III; 595 U.S. 117–121.

steps.effect: Temporarily blocks OSHA’s broad vaccine-or-test rule
steps.context: A stay pauses enforcement while litigation continues. The Court distinguished general public-health risk from workplace risks tied to particular occupations; its interim ruling concerned the broad standard before it.

steps.note: On the same day, the Court stays injunctions against the Medicare/Medicaid staff-vaccination rule, allowing enforcement while review continues. Patient health-and-safety authority supports this rule; it is a different statutory setting from OSHA’s broad employer mandate.

reviewSources.label: Per curiam Parts II-A and III; 595 U.S. 92–96.

steps.effect: Lets the health-facility vaccination rule take effect
steps.context: The Court stayed the lower courts’ injunctions. In practical terms, that allowed the vaccination rule to operate during further review—the opposite immediate result from staying the rule itself.

steps.note: For this extraordinary claim of agency power, a plausible statutory reading was insufficient. EPA needed clear congressional authorization for the authority it asserted.
steps.effect: Requires clear authorization for the asserted EPA power

steps.note: The HEROES Act’s power to “waive or modify” did not authorize this mass loan-cancellation plan. Justice Barrett separately explained major questions as part of reading statutory language in context.
steps.effect: Rejects the loan-cancellation plan under the HEROES Act

timelines.guide: The issue is whether Congress gave the agency this particular power. A program’s size alone does not decide the case. Compare the statute, the power claimed, and the setting. The two vaccination decisions reached different interim results under different statutes. A stay ruling pauses or permits action while litigation continues; it is not automatically a final merits judgment.

reviewSources.label: Roberts opinion Parts II-A-2 and II-B; Kagan concurrence pp. 1–2; opinion joining line.

timelines.title: Which jobs and benefits receive due-process protection?
timelines.question: Does the person have a protected interest before we ask what hearing is required?
timelines.anchor: what counts as a protected interest
timelines.now: Look for a legitimate entitlement grounded in law or established understandings, or a protected liberty interest. Labels such as “privilege” do not decide the question. Once protection exists, constitutional minimums govern the procedure for deprivation; the government cannot define them away in the statute creating the benefit.

steps.note: The D.C. Circuit treated government employment as a privilege outside ordinary due-process protection. An evenly divided Supreme Court affirmed without a controlling rationale; Roth later rejected the privilege premise.
steps.fate: Its right/privilege premise was rejected in Roth (1972)
steps.effect: Applies the historical job-as-privilege approach

steps.note: Officials lacked clear congressional or presidential authority for the secret-evidence clearance procedure that harmed Greene’s private employment. The Court left the constitutional question open.
steps.effect: Rejects unauthorized secret-evidence clearance procedures

steps.note: The Court allowed this cook’s exclusion from a naval installation without a hearing. It assessed the government’s military function and her particular employment interest.
steps.effect: Allows the naval-base exclusion without a hearing

steps.note: Recipients had a statutory entitlement to welfare benefits. The government therefore had to provide the required opportunity to challenge termination before stopping payment.
steps.effect: Treats welfare benefits as a protected entitlement

steps.note: Property requires a legitimate entitlement grounded in independent law or understandings. Roth’s appointment protected his existing term, but neither its terms nor state law or university policy entitled him to renewal. Nonrenewal therefore triggered no property-based hearing right on this record.
steps.effect: Finds no entitlement to another appointment year
steps.context: Roth completed the year his appointment protected. The dispute concerned another year, which no contract term, state rule, or university policy guaranteed on this record. His separate allegation of retaliation was not resolved by this procedural ruling.

steps.note: Formal tenure is not the only possible source of job protection. Established, mutually understood rules or practices may create an entitlement to continued employment.
steps.effect: Allows an entitlement based on established understandings

steps.note: Only three Justices thought a statute’s job protection necessarily came with whatever procedural limits the statute supplied. Six rejected that theory, although they differed over the procedures required.
steps.fate: Rejected by the Court in Loudermill (1985)
steps.effect: Divides over whether statutory procedure defines the right

steps.note: State law can protect a public employee’s job, but it cannot set aside the Constitution’s minimum procedures for taking that job away.
steps.effect: Separates the protected job from the procedure for removal

steps.note: Eligibility alone did not create an entitlement to emergency shelter where limited supply and unrestricted official choice left no guaranteed benefit.
steps.effect: Finds no entitlement where officials retain discretion

steps.note: The Colorado court looked at the rules controlling officials, not simply a “no entitlement” label. Funded benefits could be protected when officials could not deny them to eligible recipients.
steps.effect: Recognizes an entitlement despite a contrary label

timelines.guide: A valuable job or benefit is not automatically a protected entitlement. Look for law, contract terms, or established understandings that limit officials’ freedom to deny it. A protected liberty interest is a separate route. First identify the interest; only then decide what process is due. Loudermill separates the source of job protection from constitutional procedure.

timelines.title: What process must come before a loss?
timelines.question: Must government hear the person first, and what kind of hearing is enough?
timelines.anchor: how much process is due
timelines.now: General policymaking ordinarily does not require an individual constitutional hearing for everyone affected. For a protected individual interest, the procedure depends on the decision and the Mathews balance. An informal response before the loss plus fuller review afterward may suffice; a statute can separately require more.

steps.note: A paving assessment singled out particular property owners on individual grounds. They needed notice and a meaningful opportunity to present argument and evidence before it became final.
steps.effect: Requires a hearing for individualized assessments

steps.note: Due process did not require a separate hearing for every owner before Denver’s across-the-board assessment increase. The ruling concerns that constitutional claim; it does not erase participation procedures a statute independently requires.
steps.effect: Allows a citywide change without individual hearings

reviewSources.label: 239 U.S. 444–446: constitutional issue and contrast with Londoner

steps.note: Before ending these welfare benefits, the agency had to allow an oral response, presentation of evidence, questioning of adverse witnesses, and an impartial decisionmaker.
steps.effect: Requires a hearing before welfare benefits end

steps.note: For these disability benefits, a written chance to review and answer the evidence before termination, followed by later hearing and review, was sufficient. The Court weighed the private interest, error risk and useful safeguards, and government burdens.
steps.effect: Allows written process before disability benefits end
steps.context: An “evidentiary hearing” here means a fuller proceeding of the kind discussed in Goldberg. The Court did not approve termination with no notice, no access to the evidence, and no chance to respond.

reviewSources.label: 424 U.S. 333–335, 345–349: balancing, pretermination access and response, and later review

steps.note: School paddling affected liberty, but the Court found Florida’s legal limits and later remedies sufficient in this setting. It did not require a prior hearing or approve every alleged beating.
steps.effect: Accepts later remedies for this school-paddling dispute

steps.note: Before a disputed utility bill led to shutoff, the customer needed notice of how to object and a chance to speak to someone with authority to correct an error.
steps.effect: Requires a meaningful way to contest a utility bill

steps.note: Before dismissing this protected employee, officials had to give notice of the charges, explain the evidence, and allow a response. A fuller hearing could follow afterward.
steps.effect: Requires a chance to respond before dismissal

steps.note: Before ordering temporary reinstatement of the whistleblower, the agency had to disclose the substance of the evidence and let the employer respond. A full trial-like hearing was unnecessary.
steps.effect: Requires an employer response before temporary reinstatement

steps.note: A creditor sought to attach a home before judgment. Applying a modified Mathews balance, the Court rejected attachment without adequate notice or exceptional circumstances justifying the omission.
steps.effect: Rejects attachment without adequate prior safeguards

steps.note: After a lawful property seizure, officials must take reasonable steps to notify the owner. They need not also explain return procedures already available in published law.
steps.effect: Requires seizure notice, not a guide to published remedies

steps.note: For this withheld contract payment, an ordinary breach-of-contract lawsuit could fully protect the claim. Due process did not also require a prior administrative hearing.
steps.effect: Accepts a contract lawsuit as adequate process

timelines.guide: A hearing can be a chance to respond in writing, an informal meeting, or a proceeding with witnesses. It need not always resemble a trial. First distinguish a general policy from a decision about particular people. Mathews then weighs the person’s interest, the risk of error and value of added safeguards, and the government’s burdens.

timelines.title: When an agency may decide a case without a jury
timelines.question: Which disputes require a jury in federal court rather than a binding agency decision?
timelines.anchor: what Congress may send to an agency without a jury
timelines.now: Jarkesy requires a federal-court jury for the SEC fraud penalties before it and distinguishes Atlas Roofing’s OSHA setting. FCC v. AT&T (2026) allows nonconclusive agency findings where collection requires a fresh jury trial in court. Ask what the claim is, what remedy is sought, and what legal force the agency’s decision has.

steps.note: The executive could use the historical summary process to collect this debt from a revenue officer. The case recognizes a category of public-rights matters outside ordinary Article III trials.
steps.effect: Allows executive resolution of this public debt

steps.note: Congress could assign OSHA’s new workplace-safety duties and penalties to agency adjudication without a jury. Jarkesy later distinguished this setting from SEC fraud penalties; a new statutory label alone does not resolve the jury question.
steps.fate: Distinguished, not overruled, in Jarkesy (2024)
steps.effect: Allows agency adjudication of OSHA safety penalties

reviewSources.label: 430 U.S. 442–443 syllabus: OSHA duties, remedies, and stated holding; compare Jarkesy (2024)
Jarkesy majority, slip pp. 18–26; targeted passages checked in the preceding audit

steps.note: The government’s civil-penalty claim required a jury to decide liability. The Seventh Amendment did not also require the jury to set the penalty amount.
steps.effect: Requires a jury on civil-penalty liability

steps.note: Calling the fraudulent-conveyance action a bankruptcy “core proceeding” did not remove the jury right. The traditional legal claim against a nonclaimant remained distinct from distributing the estate.
steps.effect: Requires a jury for this traditional legal claim

steps.note: SEC fraud penalties resemble a common-law legal claim and require an Article III jury. The Court distinguishes Atlas Roofing rather than overruling it; public rights and other kinds of agency adjudication remain separate questions.
steps.effect: Requires a jury for these SEC fraud penalties
steps.context: The claim and remedy were securities-fraud civil penalties. The Court did not decide the separate nondelegation and removal issues, did not find the defendants innocent, and did not invalidate every form of agency adjudication.

timelines.guide: Agency adjudication means resolving a dispute inside an agency. Article III concerns federal judicial power; the Seventh Amendment protects civil juries in covered cases. “Public rights” is a limited exception, not simply a label for every government lawsuit. Compare the claim, the remedy, and whether agency findings bind a later court.

reviewSources.label: Majority slip pp. 6–11, especially pp. 7–10; Jarkesy distinction.

timelines.title: How agencies must explain their decisions
timelines.question: When will a court reject an agency’s reasoning?
timelines.anchor: how demanding review of agency reasoning is
timelines.now: An agency must explain its actual decision using the relevant record, statutory factors, important comments, and significant reliance interests. A court normally sends a flawed discretionary decision back rather than inventing a better explanation. Policy changes need reasons, but not automatically a higher standard of justification.

steps.note: A reviewing court must evaluate the reasons the agency actually gave. It cannot save the decision by supplying a policy judgment the agency never made.
steps.effect: Rejects judicial reasons the agency never gave

steps.note: The agency need not answer every comment individually. Its explanation must reveal the major policy questions and why it chose the rule it adopted.
steps.effect: Requires an explanation of the major policy choices

steps.note: A court asks whether the agency seriously examined the problem and explained its choice. Once it did, the court would not substitute a different policy merely because it preferred one.
steps.effect: Requires the agency to examine the problem seriously

steps.note: Review had to examine the full administrative record and the relevant statutory factors. Litigation affidavits could not replace the record of the agency’s actual decision.
steps.effect: Requires review of the full administrative record

steps.note: The challenged safety requirement failed because the agency had not adequately connected it to safety and answered the concrete objections in the record.
steps.effect: Rejects an inadequately justified safety requirement

steps.note: An agency may predict that technology will improve. It must still answer objections and plausibly explain how the necessary steps can be completed in time.
steps.effect: Allows supported predictions about future technology

steps.note: Rescinding a rule requires a reasoned explanation just as adopting one does. The agency must connect evidence to its choice and consider important alternatives; lawyers cannot add missing reasons later.
steps.effect: Rejects rescission without a reasoned explanation

steps.note: The court upheld the new rule’s explained choices already affecting parties. It declined challenges to contingent provisions because those disputes were not yet ready for decision.
steps.effect: Upholds explained choices; declines premature challenges

steps.note: Changing policy does not by itself trigger a tougher test. The agency must acknowledge the change, explain it, and address important reliance or conflicting factual findings.
steps.effect: Requires reasons for change, without a higher standard

steps.note: The explanation for adding the census citizenship question did not match the record. A stated reason that conceals the actual basis does not permit meaningful judicial review.
steps.effect: Rejects a reason that does not match the record

steps.note: DHS had to consider retaining parts of DACA and the reliance it had created. A later explanation could not retroactively supply reasons missing from the original rescission.
steps.effect: Requires consideration of alternatives and reliance

steps.note: A legal error in an agency’s discretionary reasoning ordinarily requires Chenery remand; the court may not simply substitute its own corrected analysis. Narrow remand exceptions are not a general license to supply agency policy.
steps.effect: Returns a legally flawed discretionary decision to the agency

steps.note: At the stay stage, the Court found EPA likely failed to answer an important objection about the plan’s operation with fewer states. It paused enforcement while review continued.
steps.effect: Temporarily blocks a rule over an unanswered objection

timelines.guide: The court checks the agency’s actual explanation and the material before it when it acted. It does not simply choose its preferred policy. Watch for ignored evidence, unanswered important comments, unexplained changes, and reasons invented during litigation. “Remand” sends the matter back so the agency can decide again under the right rules.

timelines.title: How much evidence supports an agency’s findings?
timelines.question: When is the factual record strong enough for a court to uphold the agency?
timelines.anchor: what the substantial-evidence standard demands
timelines.now: Review asks whether the record reasonably supports the agency’s finding, including evidence against it. The cases compare how that requirement works with different statutory procedures; the D.C. Circuit’s comparison with arbitrary-and-capricious review does not erase those procedural differences. Biestek rejects an automatic evidentiary rule and insists on context.

steps.note: The court must consider the whole record, including contrary evidence and the hearing examiner’s findings. Supporting evidence cannot be evaluated in isolation.
steps.effect: Requires consideration of evidence on both sides

steps.note: The examining doctors’ written reports could support the benefits decision despite hearsay and contrary testimony. The claimant had an available opportunity to subpoena the doctors but did not use it.
steps.effect: Allows these physicians’ written reports as evidence

steps.note: The D.C. Circuit compared the factual support required under the two APA standards. It distinguished a formal record requirement from the amount of evidence needed; the procedural settings still differ.
steps.effect: Compares factual support across APA review standards

steps.note: A health standard may rely on several imperfect studies and cautious assumptions. The agency must still explain with evidence why an available additional protection was unnecessary.
steps.effect: Requires support for the chosen level of protection

steps.note: The agency could not announce one evidentiary standard but quietly require more when applying it. Its finding had to be supported under the standard it actually stated.
steps.effect: Requires evidence under the agency’s actual standard

steps.note: Courts reviewing Patent Office factfinding must use the applicable APA standard. They cannot simply use the clear-error standard for reviewing a trial judge’s findings.
steps.effect: Applies the APA’s agency-review standards

steps.note: Informal agency action still needs factual support. The explanation must rest on evidence before the agency when it acted, not unsupported assertions.
steps.effect: Requires evidence for informal agency action too

steps.note: Refusing to disclose the expert’s underlying data did not automatically make her testimony insufficient. The court assessed reliability in the circumstances and the full hearing record.
steps.effect: Rejects an automatic rule against the expert’s testimony

timelines.guide: “Substantial evidence” means enough evidence for a reasonable person to accept the finding, considered with the whole record. Contrary evidence matters too. The court reviews the agency’s factfinding rather than retrying the case. Compare the evidence offered, the chance to challenge it, and the review standard required by the governing statute.

timelines.title: When courts can review an agency’s refusal to act
timelines.question: Can someone obtain judicial review when an agency declines to enforce, make a rule, or perform a duty?
timelines.anchor: when agency inaction is reviewable
timelines.now: Identify the refusal before applying a rule. Nonenforcement is presumptively unreviewable; refusing a rulemaking petition can be reviewed deferentially; ending a benefits program can be reviewable; and a court may compel a specific legally required action. Reviewability and success on the merits remain separate.

steps.note: The statute supplied standards for reviewing the highway decision. The narrow “committed to agency discretion” exception therefore did not prevent judicial review.
steps.effect: Finds statutory standards that permit judicial review

steps.note: A union member could obtain limited review of the Secretary’s refusal to challenge an election. The court examined the stated reasons for rationality rather than retrying the election facts.
steps.effect: Allows limited review of refusal to challenge an election

steps.note: An agency’s choice not to enforce is ordinarily unreviewable. Statutory limits on enforcement discretion can overcome that presumption; the result depends on the governing law.
steps.effect: Presumes enforcement refusals are unreviewable

steps.note: A court may review a refusal to begin rulemaking, but with substantial deference. The agency still needs a reasoned explanation supported by the record.
steps.effect: Allows deferential review of a rulemaking refusal

steps.note: A court can compel an agency to perform a specific action the law requires. It cannot supervise general compliance with a broad programmatic goal.
steps.effect: Limits compelled action to a specific legal duty

steps.note: EPA had to justify refusing the rulemaking petition using the statute’s criteria. General policy preferences outside those criteria were insufficient.
steps.effect: Requires statutory reasons for refusing rulemaking

steps.note: DACA did more than passively decline enforcement: it invited applications and provided benefits. Its rescission therefore was not insulated by the ordinary presumption against reviewing nonenforcement.
steps.effect: Allows review of DACA’s rescission

timelines.guide: “The agency did nothing” can describe different legal choices. Refusing to prosecute, refusing a rulemaking petition, ending an existing program, and failing to perform a mandatory task do not share one rule. Reviewability asks whether a court may examine the decision; it does not itself mean the challenger wins.

timelines.title: Making policy by rule or by individual case
timelines.question: May an agency announce policy in a case instead of writing a general rule first?
timelines.anchor: the agency's freedom to choose rule or adjudication
timelines.now: A properly authorized agency generally may develop policy through rules or adjudication. The choice can still be abusive or unfairly retroactive. Wyman-Gordon’s rationale was divided, and National Petroleum interprets the FTC’s particular statute rather than giving every agency an unrestricted choice.

steps.note: The APA distinguishes rules, which generally have future effect, from orders produced by adjudication. That classification helps determine which procedures apply.
steps.effect: Distinguishes rules from adjudicative orders

steps.note: An authorized agency generally may develop policy through individual cases instead of issuing a general rule first. The effect on past conduct matters, but does not automatically forbid that choice.
steps.effect: Allows policy to develop through individual cases

steps.note: The Justices disagreed about the earlier prospective announcement. The Court nevertheless enforced the specific order against this company; the plurality’s rulemaking criticism was not a majority rationale.
steps.effect: Enforces the order despite a divided view of the rule

steps.note: The D.C. Circuit found power to make substantive trade-regulation rules in the FTC Act’s particular scheme. The result does not give every agency that power merely because it has a general rulemaking clause.
steps.fate: Congress confirmed the power for unfair or deceptive practices but imposed hybrid procedures in the Magnuson-Moss Act (1975)
steps.effect: Recognizes rulemaking authority under the FTC Act

steps.note: The labor Board generally may announce new principles in adjudication. Courts can still reject an abusive choice, including unfair disruption of justified reliance.
steps.effect: Allows new principles through adjudication

timelines.guide: A rule generally states policy for future application. An adjudicative order resolves a particular matter and may also develop policy. The agency needs statutory authority for the tool it uses. These cases address its choice between tools, the effect on past conduct, and the difference between a general announcement and the order actually enforced.

timelines.title: What procedure is required to make an agency rule?
timelines.question: When are written comments enough, and when is a trial-like hearing required?
timelines.anchor: what procedure rulemaking must follow
timelines.now: The governing statute and APA determine the procedure. Ordinary notice and comment has exemptions; formal rulemaking has a different trigger; formal adjudication is another category. Courts can insist on meaningful participation and reasons while respecting Vermont Yankee’s limit on inventing extra procedures.

steps.note: The APA’s ordinary framework requires notice of a proposed rule, an opportunity for written comments, and reasons for the final rule, subject to exemptions. Formal procedures have a separate statutory trigger.
steps.effect: Sets notice-and-comment requirements and exceptions

steps.note: In this on-the-record proceeding, parties needed access to the data behind the agency’s statistical summaries. They could not meaningfully challenge evidence they could not examine.
steps.effect: Requires access to data in on-the-record proceedings

steps.note: A statute’s requirement of a hearing does not automatically require formal rulemaking. The statute must call for decision on the record after a hearing, or impose an equivalent requirement.
steps.effect: Limits the trigger for formal rulemaking

steps.note: Even without full formal procedures, the governing substantial-evidence standard required a record the parties could meaningfully test.
steps.effect: Requires a record parties can meaningfully challenge

steps.note: These permit decisions were adjudications. The Ninth Circuit read their statutory “public hearing” requirement to demand formal APA procedures; it did not make general rulemaking formal whenever a statute mentions a hearing.
steps.effect: Requires formal adjudication for these permit decisions

steps.note: The agency needed to disclose the scientific basis for meaningful public comment and address objections central to the rule. Participation is ineffective when the essential data stay hidden.
steps.effect: Requires disclosure and answers to important comments

steps.note: Courts may enforce procedures required by the Constitution, APA, and governing statute. They ordinarily may not add their preferred procedures to informal rulemaking.
steps.effect: Limits court-imposed extra procedures

steps.note: The D.C. Circuit required disclosure of technical studies used to support the rule so the public could comment. Judge Kavanaugh separately questioned the basis for that requirement.
steps.effect: Requires access to technical studies used for rulemaking

steps.note: A genuine interpretive rule is exempt from APA notice and comment. Changing an earlier interpretation does not by itself remove that exemption.
steps.effect: Allows revisions of interpretive rules without comment

steps.note: Meeting the APA’s required procedures did not also require satisfying a judge-made test of open-mindedness. The ruling did not dispose of every separate substantive challenge to the exemptions.
steps.effect: Rejects an additional open-mindedness test

steps.note: At the preliminary-injunction stage, the Fifth Circuit found the challengers likely to show that the final pistol-brace rule departed too far from the proposal to provide adequate notice.
steps.effect: Finds the final brace rule likely lacked adequate notice

timelines.guide: Ordinary notice and comment lets the public respond to a proposed rule before adoption. Formal rulemaking uses additional hearing procedures when the statute requires them. Formal adjudication is a separate category. Follow what procedure the statute demands, whether participation was meaningful, and whether a court is enforcing a requirement or inventing an extra one.

timelines.title: When “guidance” must go through rulemaking
timelines.question: Is the document explaining existing law, announcing a nonbinding policy, or creating a new legal duty?
timelines.anchor: when guidance must go through notice and comment
timelines.now: Ask whether the document creates binding law, interprets an existing obligation, or announces a tentative policy. Its title is not conclusive. Perez removes an extra notice-and-comment requirement merely for changing an interpretation; it does not exempt a document that actually makes a new legislative rule.

steps.note: A policy statement announces a tentative approach rather than binding law. When the agency later applies it, the agency must justify the resulting decision rather than treat the statement as conclusive.
steps.effect: Allows nonbinding policy without notice and comment

steps.note: The FDA’s purported guidance operated as a binding contamination limit, leaving no real discretion. Calling it guidance did not excuse the rulemaking procedure its practical effect required.
steps.effect: Treats binding contamination limits as a legislative rule

steps.note: The D.C. Circuit asks whether a rule supplies an enforcement basis missing from existing law, appears in the CFR, invokes legislative authority, or amends a legislative rule. These are indicators of legislative effect; later cases do not treat publication alone as universally conclusive.

reviewSources.label: 995 F.2d 1106, 1109–1112, especially concluding four questions at 1112.

steps.effect: Separates interpretation from creation of a legal duty

steps.note: The regulation did not itself yield an eight-foot fence requirement through interpretation. Choosing that fixed height made a new rule that needed legislative-rule procedures.
steps.effect: Requires rulemaking for the fixed fence-height command

steps.note: The court treated the sightline guidance as interpretive but announced an extra procedure for substantially changing a definitive interpretation. Perez later rejected that extra procedure.
steps.fate: Its rule on revising interpretations was abrogated by Perez (2015)
steps.effect: Historically requires procedure for changed interpretations

steps.note: Guidance that settled the agency’s position and bound parties in practice counted as reviewable final action. The agency could not use it to expand existing rules without proper rulemaking.
steps.effect: Treats practically binding guidance as reviewable action

steps.note: The cleanup document’s text bound both regulated parties and the agency. Its “guidance” label therefore did not avoid the notice-and-comment requirement for a legislative rule.
steps.effect: Requires rulemaking for binding cleanup guidance

steps.note: The Court rejected the Paralyzed Veterans requirement for changing an interpretation. Genuine interpretive rules remain exempt from notice and comment whether issued for the first time or revised.
steps.effect: Removes the extra procedure for changed interpretations

steps.note: At the preliminary stage, the deferred-action program appeared to leave officials too little real discretion to be a mere policy statement. The court treated it as likely requiring notice and comment.
steps.effect: Treats DAPA as likely requiring notice and comment

steps.note: The general existing legal duty did not compel the new adoption restrictions. Because the guidance created additional requirements, the agency needed legislative-rule procedures.
steps.effect: Requires rulemaking for new adoption requirements

timelines.guide: The label on an agency document does not settle its legal effect. An interpretive rule explains an existing duty; a policy statement describes a tentative approach; a legislative rule creates binding law under delegated power. These cases ask what the document actually does. Changing an interpretation alone does not trigger extra notice and comment under Perez.

timelines.title: Who has an injury a federal court can address?
timelines.question: Has this plaintiff shown injury, a link to the defendant, and a likely remedy?
timelines.anchor: how readily a plaintiff has standing
timelines.now: A plaintiff needs a concrete personal injury, a causal connection to the challenged conduct, and relief likely to help. Statutory violations, shared concerns, or government costs do not automatically establish those elements. The decisions distinguish tangible harm, informational harm, intangible damages claims, and demands for more enforcement against others.

steps.note: Actual economic or other injury could support standing without first proving a legal entitlement against the challenged competition. Statutory permission to sue remained a separate inquiry.
steps.effect: Recognizes actual injury without a prior legal entitlement

steps.note: Environmental or aesthetic injury can count, but the group must show harm to itself or its members. A longstanding commitment to a cause is not enough.
steps.effect: Requires injury to the group or its members

steps.note: The plaintiffs needed a concrete personal injury that was actual or imminent, caused by the challenged action, and likely to be remedied by the court. Congress could not eliminate those constitutional requirements.
steps.effect: Requires injury, a causal link, and likely relief

steps.note: The legislators alleged an abstract loss of institutional power shared with other members. That did not supply their own concrete injury, even though a statute authorized the suit.
steps.effect: Rejects legislators’ abstract loss-of-power claim

steps.note: Voters denied campaign-finance information subject to statutory public disclosure suffered concrete injury because it would help them evaluate candidates. Sharing that harm with many voters does not make it an abstract grievance.
steps.effect: Recognizes concrete harm from missing disclosure

steps.note: Pollution concerns reasonably led residents to stop using the river. Civil penalties could help prevent continued violations, so payment to the Treasury did not make the remedy useless to them.
steps.effect: Recognizes reduced river use and deterrent relief

steps.note: Massachusetts’s threatened coastal land and statutory procedural right mattered to standing. The Court gave the state special consideration; it did not excuse every state from showing injury.
steps.effect: Gives Massachusetts special consideration on standing

steps.note: An injury must be both personal to the plaintiff and concrete. A procedural violation of a statute does not automatically meet the second requirement.
steps.effect: Requires a concrete as well as personal injury

steps.note: The challenged insurance provision had no penalty, and the federal government was not enforcing or threatening to enforce it. The plaintiffs could not link their asserted injuries to federal enforcement.
steps.effect: Finds no injury traceable to federal enforcement

steps.note: Every member recovering damages needs concrete injury. For intangible injury the Court asks for a close historical analogue; an unmaterialized risk alone does not support retrospective damages, though prospective relief is a separate inquiry.
steps.effect: Requires concrete injury for each damages claimant
steps.context: Damages compensate for a past injury; an injunction seeks to prevent or stop harm. An unmaterialized risk can raise different questions for those remedies. Each class member seeking damages still needs a concrete injury.

steps.note: The states could not use indirect financial costs to force the Executive to arrest more third parties. The decision addressed that kind of enforcement demand, not every lawsuit about enforcement policy.
steps.effect: Rejects the demand for more third-party arrests

timelines.guide: Standing asks whether this plaintiff may bring this dispute to federal court. Keep its three constitutional requirements separate: a concrete personal injury, a causal link to the challenged conduct, and relief likely to help. Winning standing does not establish the underlying claim. Statutory permission to sue is another question, covered in the zone-of-interests timeline.

timelines.title: Whom does the statute authorize to sue?
timelines.question: Does this plaintiff’s interest fit the particular statutory provision being enforced?
timelines.anchor: how wide the zone of interests is
timelines.now: The APA’s lenient zone-of-interests inquiry asks whether this plaintiff’s interest arguably fits the relevant statutory provision. Another statute may use a different test. Under Lexmark, this is a question of statutory permission to sue, separate from Article III standing and subject-matter jurisdiction.

steps.note: The listening public’s responsible representatives could participate in a broadcast-license renewal dispute. Participation was not reserved to economic competitors or those facing signal interference.
steps.effect: Allows listeners to participate in license renewal

steps.note: After showing actual injury, the plaintiff needed an interest arguably protected or regulated by the relevant statute. It did not have to establish a legal right against competition first.
steps.effect: Introduces the statutory zone-of-interests inquiry

steps.note: The APA’s zone-of-interests test is lenient. Interests too remote from or inconsistent with the statute’s purposes fall outside it.
steps.effect: Applies a lenient test for APA plaintiffs

steps.note: The postal-monopoly provisions protected postal revenue, not the employees’ asserted job interests. The relevant provision’s purposes controlled, rather than any injury connected to the postal service.
steps.effect: Excludes postal workers’ interests from these provisions
steps.context: Being financially harmed is relevant to constitutional injury, but does not identify which statute authorizes this plaintiff’s suit. The court still asks whether the interest fits the particular provision invoked.

steps.note: The agency director’s disagreement with a benefits award was not the kind of adverse effect required to appeal. An institutional policy interest did not automatically make the director an aggrieved party.
steps.effect: Denies the agency director a right to appeal

steps.note: The court looked to the specific statutory provision being invoked. The regulated parties’ economic interest in avoiding unnecessary restrictions could fit that provision’s purposes.
steps.effect: Looks to the particular statutory provision invoked

steps.note: The competing banks did not have to prove Congress specifically intended to benefit them. Their interest only needed to fit arguably within the membership-limit provision’s protected or regulated zone.
steps.effect: Allows competing banks to challenge the agency

steps.note: The employee fired to retaliate against his fiancée’s discrimination charge fell within Title VII’s protected interests. He was a deliberate target, not merely a bystander affected by the dispute.
steps.effect: Allows the deliberately targeted employee to sue

steps.note: The neighboring owner’s economic, environmental, and aesthetic interests arguably fit the land-acquisition statute. The lenient APA test allowed the statutory challenge to proceed.
steps.effect: Allows the neighboring landowner’s statutory challenge

steps.note: The paper suppliers’ commercial interest only happened to align with investor protection. That incidental benefit did not place them within the securities provisions’ zone of interests.
steps.effect: Excludes paper suppliers from securities-law protection

timelines.guide: Even an injured plaintiff must identify a law authorizing this kind of suit. The “zone of interests” asks whose interests the relevant provision protects or regulates. APA review uses a lenient version of that inquiry. This differs from constitutional standing and from the court’s subject-matter jurisdiction; another statute may set a different test.

timelines.title: When organizations may sue
timelines.question: Is the organization suing for injured members or for an injury to its own work?
timelines.anchor: when an organization may sue
timelines.now: For a representative suit, identify a member with standing, an interest related to the organization’s purpose, and whether individual participation is necessary. Congress can alter the third requirement. For the organization’s own suit, identify its own concrete injury; Havens does not let an organization manufacture injury simply by spending to oppose a policy.

steps.note: An association can represent members who are injured, but must actually establish their injury. Commitment to an issue cannot substitute for that showing.
steps.effect: Requires injured members, not merely a shared cause

steps.note: The housing practices allegedly impaired the organization’s existing counseling and referral services. Read that concrete injury narrowly; choosing to spend resources opposing a policy is not enough by itself.
steps.fate: Held to its context by FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine (2024)
steps.effect: Recognizes injury to the organization’s own services

steps.note: The union needed injured members, interests related to its purpose, and a claim that did not require individual participation. It did not have to use a class action instead.
steps.effect: Reaffirms the three requirements for suing for members

steps.note: Different members may prefer different outcomes without automatically defeating the association’s suit. The members it represents must still have their own standing.
steps.effect: Allows different member interests within one association

steps.note: The usual restriction on claims requiring individual members’ participation is prudential, not constitutional. Congress could therefore authorize this union’s suit for members’ lost pay.
steps.effect: Lets Congress waive the individual-participation limit

steps.note: A genuine voluntary membership organization could rely on the ordinary Hunt test. It did not additionally have to show that members controlled or funded the organization.
steps.effect: Does not require members to control or fund the group

timelines.guide: There are two routes. An association may represent members who could sue themselves, subject to the Hunt requirements. An organization may also claim its own concrete injury. Merely caring about an issue or choosing to spend money opposing a policy is not enough. Keep the members’ injury separate from the organization’s injury.

timelines.title: Reading statutes: text, context, purpose, and history
timelines.question: What evidence helps a court decide what Congress’s words mean?
timelines.anchor: the role of purpose and legislative history against text
timelines.now: These cases show several ways courts use text and context, with disagreements over purpose and legislative history. Identify what each decision actually decided instead of treating the sequence as a single binding method. Later legislation can change a statutory result, as the expert-fee example shows.

steps.note: New York’s court read the inheritance laws against the principle that a person should not profit from wrongdoing. The grandson who murdered the testator could not inherit under the will.
steps.effect: Denies inheritance to the beneficiary who murdered

steps.note: The Court excluded this church’s foreign-pastor contract despite broad statutory wording, relying on purpose, history, and context. This illustrates the decision’s historical interpretive approach.
steps.effect: Excludes the pastor’s contract despite broad wording

steps.note: The Court consulted legislative history even though the words initially appeared clear. That history helped identify which radioactive materials the water statute covered.
steps.effect: Consults legislative history to resolve the statute’s reach

steps.note: Reading “utilized” literally would sweep widely and raise constitutional concerns. The Court adopted a narrower reading that excluded the Justice Department’s use of the ABA committee.
steps.effect: Narrows the advisory-committee statute

steps.note: The statute’s provision for attorney’s fees did not cover expert fees. The Court declined to add that recovery based on purpose; Congress later partly changed the result.
steps.fate: Partly overridden by the Civil Rights Act of 1991, which allows expert fees in § 1981 and § 1981a suits
steps.effect: Excludes expert fees under the text then in force

steps.note: The Second Circuit read “any court” in context, found ambiguity, and used legislative history to exclude foreign convictions from this firearm prohibition.
steps.effect: Excludes foreign convictions under the Second Circuit’s reading

steps.note: The Supreme Court likewise excluded foreign convictions, emphasizing the presumption that Congress legislates with domestic conditions in mind. Three Justices disagreed about the text.
steps.effect: Excludes foreign convictions under a domestic-context reading

steps.note: The fee provision did not clearly warn states that accepting federal funds would make them liable for expert fees. A conference report could not supply the missing notice.
steps.effect: Requires clear notice before states owe expert fees

steps.note: The nonmechanical bump stocks at issue still required a separate trigger function for each shot. The Court therefore held they did not satisfy the statute’s machinegun definition.
steps.effect: Excludes the bump stocks at issue from “machinegun”

steps.note: Some weapon-parts kits and unfinished frames fit the statutory definitions. That was enough to reject the facial challenge to the rule; the Court did not decide every possible application.
steps.effect: Rejects a facial challenge to the gun-kit rule

timelines.guide: These cases use different interpretive tools, often together: ordinary meaning, surrounding text, statutory structure, purpose, and legislative history. They do not form a simple progression in which one tool replaces all others. Identify the exact disputed words and the outcome in each case. Clear-notice and constitutional concerns sometimes affect the reading.

timelines.title: Reading a word in the company it keeps
timelines.question: How can neighboring words or a specific list explain a broad term?
timelines.anchor: how far the associated-words canons narrow general terms
timelines.now: Look for what the neighboring words or listed examples have in common, then test that reading against the statute as a whole. The canons can explain a general phrase, but do not override stronger textual or contextual evidence.

steps.note: The surrounding list of land vehicles and the need for fair warning in criminal law kept “vehicle” from reaching a stolen airplane.
steps.effect: Excludes an airplane from the vehicle-theft statute

steps.note: After dagger, dirk, and stiletto, “other dangerous weapon” covered weapons of that stabbing kind. The rifle did not fit the listed category.
steps.effect: Excludes a rifle from the listed class of weapons

steps.note: The surrounding terms and the statute’s use of “prospectus” concerned public offerings. The privately negotiated stock-sale agreement fell outside this provision.
steps.effect: Excludes a private sale from this prospectus provision

steps.note: The Second Circuit read “negligent transmission” with “loss” and “miscarriage” of mail. It did not cover the personal injury from a package left in someone’s path.
steps.effect: Excludes a trip hazard from the postal exception

steps.note: The Supreme Court likewise rejected treating every delivery mishap as part of the postal exception. Lost, delayed, damaged, or misdelivered mail differs from this trip hazard.
steps.effect: Confirms that the postal exception does not cover this injury

steps.note: The Court read “other concerted activities” alongside organizing and collective bargaining. It did not treat the phrase as overriding enforcement of individual arbitration agreements.
steps.effect: Does not read collective lawsuits into the labor provision

timelines.guide: Noscitur a sociis means a word can take meaning from nearby words. Ejusdem generis means a general phrase following specific examples may cover the same kind of thing. First identify the list or phrase, then ask what its items share. These are aids to reading the statute in context, not automatic rules that every broad word must shrink.

timelines.title: Warranties: promised quality and implied protection
timelines.question: Which warranty fits the claimed defect?
timelines.anchor: What distinguishes an express promise from merchantability and fitness for a particular purpose?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: Express warranties arise from qualifying statements, descriptions, samples or models that form part of the bargain. Merchantability ordinarily requires a merchant dealing in goods of that kind. Fitness for a particular purpose concerns the seller’s knowledge and the buyer’s reliance on its judgment. Disclaimers and state enactments can affect each analysis.

steps.note: A seller’s knowledge of the buyer’s particular purpose and reliance can support an implied fitness warranty.
steps.effect: Protecting reliance on the seller’s selection
steps.context: Under § 2-315, the seller must have reason to know both the purpose and the buyer’s reliance on its skill or judgment to select suitable goods.

steps.note: A factual statement or description can create an express warranty without formal warranty language.
steps.effect: Recognizing factual warranty statements
steps.context: Keith treats such an affirmation as part of the bargain unless the seller proves otherwise; § 2-313 does not require a separate intent to warrant.

steps.note: Statements about a differently equipped boat and general sales praise did not warrant the performance of the boat actually sold.
steps.effect: Matching the promise to the purchased boat
steps.context: A qualifying affirmation, promise or description must relate to the purchased goods and form part of the bargain.

steps.note: Merchantability measures ordinary fitness through reasonable users’ expectations, not this particular user’s subjective hopes.
steps.effect: Measuring ordinary fitness objectively
steps.context: This inquiry concerns the product’s ordinary purpose, distinct from a fitness warranty based on reliance for a particular purpose.

steps.note: The disclaimer’s overall presentation determined whether a reasonable person should notice it.
steps.effect: Assessing a disclaimer’s presentation
steps.context: The New York provisions did not impose an absolute requirement that a written implied-warranty disclaimer appear before the signature.

timelines.guide: Use three separate paths: the seller’s factual promise, ordinary fitness, or fitness for the buyer’s particular purpose. Keith and Bayliner concern statements; Koken concerns ordinary expectations; Lewis concerns reliance on the seller’s selection. NY Drilling addresses a disclaimer.

timelines.title: A promise made after the benefit
timelines.question: Can gratitude for an earlier act make a later promise enforceable?
timelines.anchor: When can an earlier benefit support a later promise?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: A benefit supplied before a promise is not automatically a bargained-for exchange. Webb recognizes enforcement of a later promise tied to a material benefit received by the promisor; Mills and Harrington show limits and contrasting approaches. A moral reason to pay is not universally a legal obligation.

steps.note: Gratitude for an earlier benefit did not supply consideration for the later promise to pay.
steps.effect: Rejecting gratitude as consideration
steps.context: The benefit was not requested as a bargain, and no existing legal obligation of this promisor supplied the missing basis for enforcement.

steps.note: The court enforced a later payment promise tied to a material benefit personally received by the promisor.
steps.effect: Enforcing a promise after material benefit
steps.context: Saving the promisor’s life supplied the material-benefit setting. This route did not require a prior bargain; compare the contrary rescue outcome in Harrington.

steps.note: This voluntary rescue did not supply consideration for a later promise to pay for the rescuer’s injuries.
steps.effect: Rejecting a promise after voluntary rescue
steps.context: Compare Webb’s material-benefit approach. These decisions from different jurisdictions do not create one universal rule about rescue promises.

timelines.guide: Compare what the promisor received and how the court treated the later promise. Mills rejects gratitude as consideration; Webb recognizes a material-benefit route; Harrington rejects enforcement after another rescue. Different jurisdictions reach different results.

timelines.title: Restitution: paying for a retained benefit
timelines.question: When may someone recover value even without enforcing the promised bargain?
timelines.anchor: When is the value of a benefit recoverable despite the absence, breach or avoidance of a contract?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: Restitution measures a benefit received, not simply everything the claimant spent or hoped to earn. The claimant’s role matters: a party in breach, an injured party, an emergency professional and a party unwinding a mistaken agreement face different rules.

steps.note: The worker who quit could recover the employer’s retained benefit, even though he could not recover on the unfinished contract.
steps.effect: Paying a breaching worker’s net benefit
steps.context: Recovery was reduced by the harm from the breach and capped by the contract price. Quantum meruit means payment for the reasonable value of services.

steps.note: Necessary emergency professional services could earn reasonable compensation despite the patient’s inability to consent.
steps.effect: Paying for necessary emergency services
steps.context: The services had to be furnished in good faith; success was not required. The patient’s wealth could not enlarge the fee.

steps.note: A subcontractor justified in stopping after the other side’s material breach could recover the value of work already supplied.
steps.effect: Recovering value after justified termination
steps.context: Subtract payments received, but not the loss the subcontractor would have suffered by completing this losing bargain. In this holding, the contract price was not a ceiling.

steps.note: Arizona allowed the mistaken transaction to be unwound, with restitution of benefits rather than reimbursement of every reliance expense.
steps.effect: Returning benefits after rescission
steps.context: The mutual mistake concerned a basic assumption materially affecting the exchange. Without fraud or misrepresentation, the remedy did not include consequential losses from development expenditures.

timelines.guide: Identify why contract enforcement is unavailable. Britton concerns a worker who breached, Cotnam emergency services without assent, Algernon Blair justified departure after the other side’s breach, and Renner rescission for mistake. Their deductions and limits differ.

timelines.title: Writing requirements and their exceptions
timelines.question: Does this promise need a writing, and does this transaction satisfy an exception?
timelines.anchor: Which promises require a signed writing, and when can several writings, performance or reliance suffice?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: The governing statute determines the writing and any exception. Model UCC § 2-201 generally covers goods sales of $500 or more, limits enforcement to the written quantity, and recognizes specified exceptions. The cases here concern other statutory categories and jurisdiction-specific rules about writings, performance and reliance.

steps.note: California barred the writing defense where refusal to enforce would cause unconscionable reliance injury or unjust enrichment.
steps.effect: Preventing reliance-based injustice
steps.context: Monarco did not require a separate representation about supplying a writing. Other jurisdictions’ estoppel exceptions can differ.

steps.note: Related signed and unsigned documents could together satisfy the writing requirement.
steps.effect: Combining related writings
steps.context: The writings had to refer on their face to the same transaction and contain every essential term. Oral evidence could connect them and show assent; it could not supply a missing essential term.

steps.note: Under Connecticut’s rule, an agreement of indefinite duration fell outside the one-year writing requirement.
steps.effect: Excluding indefinite-duration performance
steps.context: The agreement did not expressly require performance beyond a year. How long the work would actually take did not change that statutory analysis.

steps.note: Accepting the deed bound the recipient to its mortgage-assumption clause even without the recipient’s signature.
steps.effect: Recognizing an original debt undertaking
steps.context: The promise to the grantor was an original undertaking, rather than a promise to answer for someone else’s debt within the suretyship writing rule.

steps.note: The main-purpose exception can permit an oral debt-payment promise made to secure the promisor’s own benefit.
steps.effect: Applying the promisor’s main-purpose exception
steps.context: The court examined the whole transaction; releasing the original debtor was not required.

steps.note: The buyers’ performance could establish the oral land-sale agreement despite the missing writing.
steps.effect: Recognizing land-sale part performance
steps.context: Under the test applied, an informed outsider would naturally and reasonably infer a land contract. The conduct need not have only that possible explanation; equity could supply a fair price and reasonable time.

timelines.guide: Start with the statutory category. Klewin concerns the one-year provision; Langman and Central Ceilings concern another person’s debt; Beaver concerns land. Crabtree addresses combined writings, and Monarco reliance-based estoppel. Do not transfer one category’s exception to another.

timelines.title: Capacity: minors, mental illness and guardianship
timelines.question: Could this person incur the obligation, and what follows if it is avoided?
timelines.anchor: Who may avoid an agreement because of incapacity, and what qualifications govern avoidance?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: Minority, mental incapacity and adjudicated guardianship are distinct grounds for challenging contractual duties. Ask which test applies, what the other party knew or should have known, and whether payment or restitution is available. The cases do not supply one rule for every minor or every mental-health condition.

steps.note: Mental weakness alone did not establish incapacity to understand this transaction’s nature and effect.
steps.effect: Testing understanding of the transaction
steps.context: A person who retained that capacity but was vulnerable still needed to prove fraud or overreaching under the test applied.

steps.note: Understanding the transaction was not the only capacity question: mental illness could prevent reasonable action concerning it.
steps.effect: Considering inability to act reasonably
steps.context: The other party needed reason to know of the condition. This is distinct from treating every unwise decision as incapacity.

steps.note: A minor returning goods after a fair purchase could owe reasonable deductions for use, depreciation or damage.
steps.effect: Accounting for a minor’s use of goods
steps.context: The rule addressed a purchase without seller overreaching, after the minor paid and used the item. Willful or negligent damage could also affect the refund.

steps.note: Hawaii’s employment statutes defeated the ordinary infancy defense, but the arbitration clause still failed.

reviewSources.label: 110 Haw. 525–534; original opinion May 25, 2006 (later corrected May 30)

steps.effect: Applying an employment-specific infancy exception
steps.context: The employee was seventeen. The majority separately found no binding assent and consideration for the handbook arbitration provision; rejecting one defense did not validate the clause.

steps.note: The existing guardianship adjudication prevented enforcement of this purchase and the seller’s restitution claim.
steps.effect: Giving effect to adjudicated guardianship
steps.context: The order supplied constructive public notice, even though the seller lacked actual knowledge. This concerns adjudicated guardianship, not merely an undiagnosed weakness in judgment.

timelines.guide: Cundick and Ortelere use different capacity inquiries; Kenai concerns an existing guardianship adjudication. Dodson concerns a minor returning used goods. Douglass shows how a specific employment statute can change the infancy analysis without validating an arbitration clause.

timelines.title: Pressure: duress and undue influence
timelines.question: Did wrongful pressure or unfair persuasion undermine consent?
timelines.anchor: When does pressure or unfair persuasion make an apparent agreement voidable?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: Economic duress asks about wrongful pressure and reasonable alternatives. Undue influence asks about susceptibility and unfair persuasion that overcomes a person’s will. An unwanted bargain or economic difficulty alone does not answer either inquiry; the circumstances and applicable law control.

steps.note: Excessive persuasion exploiting weakness or distress can overcome consent and support rescission.
steps.effect: Examining excessive persuasion
steps.context: Undue influence need not include misrepresentation or a confidential relationship. The inquiry concerns the interaction between susceptibility and the pressure used.

steps.note: Threatening to withhold goods already owed left the buyer without timely replacements or an adequate breach remedy.
steps.effect: Recognizing economic duress
steps.context: Those circumstances supported economic duress and avoidance of the price modification; a threat or difficult bargain alone does not supply the entire test.

steps.note: California’s duress and undue-influence tests require different kinds of proof from the party seeking rescission.
steps.effect: Separating duress from undue influence
steps.context: Duress concerns a wrongful act inducing agreement without a reasonable alternative. Undue influence concerns susceptibility and excessive pressure that overbears the will.

timelines.guide: Compare the problem creating the pressure. Austin involves threatened supply cutoff and unavailable timely alternatives; Odorizzi involves susceptibility and excessive persuasion. Martinez-Gonzalez distinguishes the tests and the proof required under California law.

timelines.title: Public policy and the limits of enforcement
timelines.question: Would enforcing this promise undermine a policy the law protects?
timelines.anchor: When does public policy justify denying enforcement, and when would that remedy go too far?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: Nonenforcement requires an identifiable legal policy and attention to what enforcement would do. Statutes, professional duties and the transaction’s purpose can point to different results. Keep historical holdings separate from later legislation, especially the dating-service, surrogacy and noncompete examples.

steps.note: A large profit or eventual government purchase did not by itself make the contract contrary to public policy.
steps.effect: Rejecting a vague policy objection
steps.context: The agreement was made freely at arm’s length without fraud. A policy objection needed support in identifiable law and precedent.

steps.note: The allegation of dismissal for insisting on statutory compliance could support a wrongful-discharge tort claim.
steps.effect: Recognizing a public-policy discharge claim
steps.context: The employee had to identify a demonstrably improper reason violating a clear public-policy mandate. This was a claim at the pleading stage, not a finding that the allegations were proved.

steps.note: A term can conflict with strong statutory policy even when no statute expressly forbids that exact term.
steps.effect: Protecting statutory policy against waiver
steps.context: The court looked to the statute’s purpose, history and overall scheme when deciding whether to enforce the agreement.

steps.note: The seller’s active assistance in an improper use could defeat its claim for payment.
steps.effect: Refusing aid to unlawful performance
steps.context: A buyer’s intended misuse alone ordinarily would not suffice. The distinction is between knowing about that use and acting to further it.

steps.note: The court rejected this paid-surrogacy agreement; custody required a separate best-interests decision.
steps.effect: Rejecting this paid-surrogacy agreement
steps.context: The agreement committed the mother before birth to surrender the child and terminate parental rights, contrary to the adoption statutes and public policy then applied. This historical ruling does not establish today’s law for every surrogacy arrangement.

steps.note: Illinois generally denied in-house counsel a common-law retaliatory-discharge claim against the employer-client.
steps.effect: Applying the lawyer-employment limit
steps.context: The court relied on the lawyer’s mandatory professional duties to protect the policy at issue. This is a specific lawyer-employment rule, not the rule for every at-will employee.

steps.note: An alleged antitrust conspiracy did not automatically invalidate a contract lawful on its face.
steps.effect: Testing what enforcement would accomplish
steps.context: The question was whether enforcing payment would itself enforce the precise conduct forbidden by antitrust law. The court did not award the unpaid price merely by rejecting automatic invalidity.

steps.note: The court applied New York’s 2005 dating-service pricing and referral rules to these contracts.
steps.effect: Applying the 2005 dating-service statute
steps.context: Without a promised number of monthly referrals, the statute as applied capped the charge at $25. An injured consumer could recover actual damages or $50, whichever was greater. This is the historical statutory regime applied in the case.

steps.note: In 2022, Wyoming refused to rewrite an unreasonable noncompete to make it enforceable.
steps.fate: Later developments: the 2023 appeal preserved a severable attorney-fee clause; invalidating the noncompete did not void the whole contract. Wyoming’s 2025 legislation separately restricts noncompetes in contracts entered on or after July 1, 2025, with specified exceptions; it expressly leaves earlier contracts unaltered.

reviewSources.label: Circle C Resources v. Hassler, 2023 WY 54, ¶¶11–20, 37
2025 Wyoming Session Laws ch.170, §§1–3, printed pp.392–394 (PDF pp.406–408)

steps.effect: Refusing to rewrite a noncompete
steps.context: The employer bore the burden of justifying a presumptively invalid restraint. Unreasonable duration or geography defeated this covenant; the later fee-clause decision and 2025 statute are separate developments.

timelines.guide: Identify the actual policy and the proposed remedy. These cases concern distinct problems: unlawful use of goods, statutory rights, employment retaliation, surrogacy and restraints on competition. A policy objection does not automatically invalidate every term or determine custody or damages.

timelines.title: Breach: stop, accept, or allow a cure?
timelines.question: Is this failure serious enough to justify withholding or ending performance?
timelines.anchor: When may a party withhold or terminate performance, and when must it allow cure?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: Not every breach permits termination. Materiality, substantial performance and the parties’ dependent duties matter in the common-law cases. Goods transactions have separate rules for rejection, cure and revocation of acceptance. A mistaken decision to stop performing can itself be a breach.

steps.note: An innocent, trivial departure did not forfeit payment for substantially completed construction.
steps.effect: Paying for substantial performance
steps.context: Damages still compensated the defect. Where replacement cost was grossly disproportionate to the benefit, the measure was the loss in value.

steps.note: Stopping performance over a failure that is not material can make the terminating party the breacher.
steps.effect: Testing whether termination was justified
steps.context: Materiality depends on several circumstances. A party cannot safely treat every unsatisfactory performance as grounds for repudiating the whole agreement.

steps.note: The subcontractor’s material breach justified withholding the progress payment.
steps.effect: Withholding payment after material breach
steps.context: The duties were treated as dependent. The subcontractor could not turn that justified withholding into a new breach excusing its own departure.

steps.note: A qualifying seller had an opportunity to replace the nonconforming goods under UCC § 2-508(2).
steps.effect: Allowing a qualifying seller to cure
steps.context: The seller reasonably believed the tender would be acceptable and gave timely notice of intent to cure. This qualification limits the buyer’s otherwise available rejection right.

steps.note: A termination notice period did not itself promise an opportunity to cure.
steps.effect: Distinguishing notice from cure rights
steps.context: The terminating party was not confined to its initially stated reason unless the other side had relied on that reason to its detriment.

steps.note: Substantial impairment supported revoking acceptance; the goods did not have to be completely useless.
steps.effect: Revoking acceptance for substantial impairment
steps.context: The buyer’s own needs mattered, but objective evidence had to establish the impairment. The case concerned a nonconformity the seller failed to cure in time.

timelines.guide: First identify the governing regime. Jacob & Youngs, Walker and K & G concern materiality and substantial performance. Bartus and Jorgensen concern UCC remedies for goods. New England Structures separately asks what the termination notice promised.

timelines.title: Before performance: refusal, insecurity and readiness
timelines.question: Has the other side refused to perform, or merely raised a concern?
timelines.anchor: When can a party act before performance is due, and what must it show about its own performance?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: A clear anticipatory refusal differs from a report of difficulty. For goods, UCC § 2-609 permits a written assurance demand on reasonable grounds; the response period must be reasonable and at most thirty days. Section 2-610 addresses substantially impairing repudiation. The claimant’s readiness and any prevention of performance remain separate questions.

steps.note: An unequivocal refusal before the due date allowed an immediate damages action.
steps.effect: Allowing suit before the due date
steps.context: The injured party could treat the contract as breached and stop future performance, or instead await the performance date.

steps.note: The buyer’s competing purchases made performance harder, but did not legally excuse the seller’s breach.
steps.effect: Distinguishing difficulty from prevention
steps.context: Actual prevention is different from added difficulty or expense; an agreed exclusive source could change the analysis.

steps.note: Reporting difficulty obtaining materials and asking for help did not amount to an unequivocal refusal to perform.
steps.effect: Requiring an unequivocal refusal
steps.context: Anticipatory repudiation required an absolute refusal or a distinct, positive statement of inability—not merely a concern about performance.

steps.note: Repudiation excused tender, but not proof that the claimant was ready, willing and able to perform.
steps.effect: Requiring readiness despite excused tender
steps.context: To recover damages for the option or first-refusal right, the claimant had to establish that ability within the option period.

steps.note: A demand for adequate assurance required reasonable grounds for insecurity.
steps.effect: Testing grounds for an assurance demand
steps.context: Although insecurity and adequate assurance ordinarily raise factual questions, summary judgment was possible when no reasonable jury could find the demand justified or the response inadequate.

timelines.guide: Hochster permits action on an early refusal. McCloskey distinguishes difficulty from refusal; By-Lo asks when assurance may be demanded. Iron Trade concerns alleged prevention, and Kanavos requires proof that the claimant could have performed.

timelines.title: Transferring rights and performance duties
timelines.question: What can be transferred, and how is the other contracting party protected?
timelines.anchor: What rights and duties move to another person, and what limits protect the original obligor?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: Transfers do not erase the original bargain’s protections. Assignment may face increased-burden and consent limits. Delegation under model UCC § 2-210 does not release the original promisor, and the other party’s substantial interest can prevent substitution. An assignee may take rights subject to existing contractual defenses.

steps.note: The indemnity right could not be assigned in a way that materially increased the indemnitor’s risk.
steps.effect: Preventing an increased indemnity risk
steps.context: The proposed substitution increased the likelihood of having to pay. Assignment cannot simply erase the protections built into the original undertaking.

steps.note: The distributor could not delegate performance to the manufacturer’s competitor or its wholly owned subsidiary without consent.
steps.effect: Rejecting delegation to a competitor
steps.context: Under UCC § 2-210(1), the identity of the performer mattered in this exclusive distributorship.

steps.note: An unauthorized assignment could be effective even though making it breached a consent clause.
steps.effect: Distinguishing assignment power from breach
steps.context: The court distinguished a contractual prohibition from language making an assignment void or ineffective. The actual wording controls that distinction.

steps.note: The assignee took the claim subject to the original contract’s terms and transaction-based defenses.
steps.effect: Preserving defenses against an assignee
steps.context: Under UCC § 9-404(a)(1), those defenses did not depend on when the debtor received notice of the assignment.

timelines.guide: Assignment transfers a right to receive performance; delegation concerns who performs a duty. Compare increased risk in Kingston, a competing distributor in Sally Beauty, a consent clause in Bel-Ray, and defenses against an assignee in Delacy.

timelines.title: Mistake: assumptions, risk and rescission
timelines.question: Was a basic assumption wrong, and which party bore that risk?
timelines.anchor: When does a mistaken assumption permit avoidance, and who bore the risk?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: A mistaken assumption does not automatically undo a contract. Ask whether it was basic and material, whether the claimant bore the risk, and whether rescission remains available. Even when the deal is unwound, restitution of benefits differs from reimbursing every reliance expense.

steps.note: The seller could not undo this completed sale merely because both parties had underestimated the article’s nature and value.
steps.effect: Leaving an uncertain-value sale intact
steps.context: The item delivered was the item sold. Without fraud, inadequate price alone did not justify recovery under the historical rule applied.

steps.note: The Michigan court distinguished a mistake about the bargain’s substance from one merely about quality.
steps.effect: Distinguishing substance from quality
steps.context: The historical test could permit avoidance even after completion. Read the later Lenawee treatment before treating this distinction as Michigan’s general test.
steps.fate: Lenawee County v. Messerly (Michigan, 1982) limited Sherwood’s substance-versus-quality distinction to its facts and adopted a basic-assumption and risk-allocation analysis.

steps.note: A buyer who keeps goods beyond a reasonable time without rejecting them cannot afterward rescind the sale for an innocent misrepresentation about a quality such as authorship; any remaining remedy is damages.
steps.effect: Denying rescission after prolonged retention

steps.note: The shared mistake was basic and material, but the buyers bore its risk and could not rescind.
steps.effect: Allocating the risk of mutual mistake
steps.context: Michigan considered the as-is clause when allocating the risk of the property’s undiscovered sewage defect. The opinion separately notes that an as-is clause does not bar a fraud or misrepresentation claim; those findings were not appealed here.
