steps.note: Arizona allowed the mistaken transaction to be unwound, with restitution of benefits rather than reimbursement of every reliance expense.
steps.effect: Limiting relief to returned benefits
steps.context: The mutual mistake concerned a basic assumption materially affecting the exchange. Without fraud or misrepresentation, the remedy did not include consequential losses from development expenditures.

timelines.guide: Compare uncertainty about what was sold with a shared mistaken assumption. Wood and Sherwood use older formulations; Lenawee focuses on a basic assumption and risk allocation. Leaf adds a delay problem, while Renner addresses what must be returned after rescission.

timelines.title: Notice: a reasonable chance to learn of the case
timelines.question: What does due process require when the government gives notice?
timelines.anchor: What does due process require when the government gives notice?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: Choose a method reasonably likely to inform the affected person in the circumstances. Known addresses and known delivery problems matter. Actual receipt is not always required, but returned mail may call for feasible additional steps. Class notice and probate deadlines also have setting-specific requirements.

steps.note: Notice must reasonably try to tell affected people about the proceeding and give them a chance to object. A method too unlikely to reach known people is inadequate.
steps.effect: Notice must reasonably inform affected people
steps.context: Before a proceeding that is to be accorded finality, due process requires notice reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances, to apprise interested parties of the pendency of the action and afford them an opportunity to present their objections.

steps.note: Posting eviction papers on apartment doors was inadequate where removal was common and mail could improve the chance of notice.
steps.effect: Unreliable door posting needs a better method
steps.context: Notice must be reasonably calculated under the circumstances to reach the person affected; posting an eviction notice on a tenant's door is inadequate where posted notices are known to be frequently removed and feasible measures such as mail could improve reliability.

steps.note: A mortgagee identifiable from public records needed direct notice of a tax sale, such as mailed notice or personal service; publication alone was inadequate.
steps.effect: Identifiable mortgagee needs direct tax-sale notice
steps.context: When a mortgagee is reasonably identifiable from a publicly recorded mortgage, due process requires that publication of a tax sale be supplemented by notice mailed to its last known available address or by personal service.

steps.note: Absent members of a money-damages class could be bound without minimum contacts if they received notice, a chance to participate and opt out, and adequate representation.
steps.effect: Absent damages-class members need procedural protections
steps.context: A forum may bind absent plaintiff-class members on money claims without minimum contacts if they receive the best practicable notice, a chance to be heard, a chance to opt out, and adequate representation; but it may apply its own law only to claims with sufficient forum contacts.

steps.note: Known or reasonably identifiable creditors needed reliable direct notice before this court-triggered probate deadline extinguished their claims. Publication sufficed for creditors not reasonably identifiable.
steps.effect: Known creditors need direct probate notice
steps.context: When a probate nonclaim period is triggered by court-ordered proceedings and extinguishes a creditor's claim, due process requires notice by mail or a comparably reliable means to creditors who are known or reasonably ascertainable; publication suffices only for the rest.

steps.note: Due process required a reasonable attempt to notify the prisoner, not proof that he personally received the mailed forfeiture notice.
steps.effect: Reasonable effort does not require actual receipt
steps.context: The adequacy of notice is judged under Mullane's standard of notice reasonably calculated under the circumstances, which requires a reasonable effort to inform the interested person rather than proof of actual receipt.

steps.note: When tax-sale mail came back unclaimed, the state had to try additional reasonable notification steps if practical before selling the property.
steps.effect: Returned mail calls for feasible additional steps
steps.context: When a mailed notice of a tax sale is returned unclaimed before the sale, due process requires the state to take additional reasonable steps to notify the owner if it is practicable to do so.

timelines.guide: Notice tells someone that a proceeding may affect their rights. The question is whether the chosen method reasonably tries to reach them, not whether every notice actually arrives. Follow what changes when an address is known, a delivery method is unreliable or mailed notice comes back unclaimed.

timelines.title: Service: delivering the lawsuit in an authorized way
timelines.question: Who can receive service, and why does actual notice not always cure an invalid method?
timelines.anchor: Who can receive service, and why does actual notice not always cure an invalid method?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: Ask what method the applicable rule authorizes and whether the recipient qualifies. Actual awareness does not automatically repair defective service. For foreign defendants, also ask whether a treaty applies; service on a foreign state has its own statutory sequence and delivery requirements.

steps.note: A party could not lure a nonresident into the state through a lawyer’s trickery and then rely on personal service obtained there.
steps.effect: Trickery invalidates personal service
steps.context: A party cannot secure personal service on an otherwise out-of-reach nonresident by fraud, trickery, artifice or a wrongful device, used by the party or someone acting for the party, that induces the person to enter the court's territorial jurisdiction; such service will be set aside.

steps.note: The appointed agent’s prompt forwarding of the papers made service valid under the Federal Rule. The decision left failed-notice and broader due-process questions open.
steps.effect: Appointed agent’s prompt forwarding validates service
steps.context: The appointed agent actually accepted the papers and promptly sent them to the defendants. The Court reserved the consequences of failed notification and did not resolve a general due-process challenge to every contractual jurisdiction term.

steps.note: Service on this sufficiently integrated corporate employee was valid without express appointment. The company’s later internal loss of the papers did not excuse its default.
steps.effect: Integrated corporate employee can receive service
steps.context: Service on a corporation is valid when delivered to an employee so integrated with the organization that he will know what to do with the papers, even without express authorization; losing the papers internally afterward is not excusable neglect.

steps.note: The Hague Service Convention did not apply when valid service on the foreign corporation was completed domestically, with no required transmission abroad.
steps.effect: Domestic service can avoid treaty transmission rules
steps.context: The Hague Service Convention applies only when the forum's internal law requires documents to be transmitted abroad to complete service; where valid service on a foreign corporation is complete domestically, the Convention does not apply.

steps.note: A person can have more than one settled home for service. This does not mean actual notice repairs service at an otherwise invalid location.
steps.effect: More than one settled home can qualify
steps.context: A person may have more than one dwelling or usual place of abode for service of process, provided each has sufficient signs of permanence; actual notice does not cure service that is otherwise void.

steps.note: Delivering papers to an unauthorized recipient did not become valid service simply because the defendant learned of the case; the resulting default judgment was void.
steps.effect: Actual receipt does not cure unauthorized delivery
steps.context: A default judgment entered without valid service is void for lack of personal jurisdiction and must be vacated; actual receipt of the papers cannot by itself cure delivery to someone who is not the defendant's officer or authorized agent.

steps.note: For this statutory method of serving a foreign state, the packet had to go to the foreign minister’s office abroad—not the state’s U.S. embassy.
steps.effect: Foreign-state packet must go to minister’s office
steps.context: Under § 1608(a)(3) of the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act, a service packet for a foreign state must be mailed directly to the foreign minister at the minister's office in the foreign state, not to the state's embassy in the United States.

timelines.guide: Service formally delivers the papers that bring a defendant into the lawsuit. Knowing about the case is not always enough: the right papers must reach an authorized person through a permitted method. The cases address deception, agents, homes, corporations and the additional rules for service involving foreign countries.

timelines.title: Discovery: what information can parties obtain?
timelines.question: What can be discovered, by whom, and on what showing?
timelines.anchor: What can be discovered, by whom, and on what showing?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: Ordinary discovery must concern a claim or defense, avoid privilege and be proportional to the case. The information need not itself be admissible at trial. Medical exams, testimony preserved before suit, early identifying requests and use of depositions at trial each add distinct requirements.

steps.note: A party’s medical examination requires a genuine dispute about the particular condition and good cause for that examination. Being a defendant does not by itself prevent examination.
steps.effect: Examinations need genuine dispute and good cause
steps.context: Rule 35 permits a mental or physical examination of any party, defendant as well as plaintiff, but only on an affirmative showing that each condition is genuinely in controversy and that there is good cause for each particular examination.

steps.note: A deposition’s “discovery” label does not prevent trial use. For the distance-based route, Rule 32’s notice, admissibility and absence requirements still matter.
steps.effect: Trial use depends on Rule 32, not deposition label
steps.context: Rule 32(a)(4)(B) permits use when a witness is more than 100 miles away or outside the United States, unless the offering party procured that absence. Other Rule 32 requirements, including notice/opportunity to participate and evidentiary limits, also apply.

steps.note: Rule 27 preserves testimony at risk of being lost before suit. It is not a general way to investigate whether the plaintiff has a claim or whom to sue.
steps.effect: Pre-suit deposition preserves endangered testimony
steps.context: Federal Rule 27(a) permits a deposition before suit only to perpetuate testimony that might otherwise be lost; it is not a device for pre-complaint discovery of the facts or of whom to sue.

steps.note: Calling a written question a contention interrogatory did not automatically justify refusing it. This court required the available supporting facts, with later supplementation as needed.
steps.effect: Contention questions are not automatically premature
steps.context: The party resisting discovery bears the burden of justifying its refusal, and labelling an interrogatory a contention interrogatory does not make it premature; a party must answer with the facts it presently has and may amend or supplement later.

steps.note: This products-liability discovery ruling weighed relevance and proportionality, including how similar the other product designs were to the product in the lawsuit.
steps.effect: Product-design requests face relevance and proportionality
steps.context: Under Rule 26(b)(1) discovery must be relevant and proportional to the needs of the case, and in a products-liability case discovery of other designs is measured on a sliding scale of similarity to the product at issue.

steps.note: This court allowed early discovery to identify a defendant on a good-cause showing, with jurisdictional support and protections for the person being identified.
steps.effect: Early identifying discovery may proceed with safeguards
steps.context: A court may allow discovery before the Rule 26(f) conference on good cause, meaning the discovery is needed for the suit to progress, if the plaintiff has a good-faith basis for personal jurisdiction, and may attach conditions protecting the person to be identified.

timelines.guide: Discovery is the process of obtaining information for a lawsuit. Relevance and proportionality set the ordinary scope, but each method has additional conditions. These cases compare medical examinations, depositions, written questions and requests made before ordinary discovery begins; they do not create one test for every request.

reviewSources.label: Rule 26(b)(1); Advisory Committee Note to 2015 amendment

timelines.title: Discovery protections for legal advice and trial preparation
timelines.question: Which lawyer-related communications and materials are protected, and what are the limits?
timelines.anchor: Which lawyer-related communications and materials are protected, and what are the limits?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: Keep confidential legal advice separate from litigation preparation. Attorney-client privilege and work product protect different things. Fact work product can sometimes be obtained on the required showing of need and hardship, while counsel’s mental impressions receive stronger protection. An adverse privilege ruling does not ordinarily create an immediate collateral-order appeal.

steps.note: A lawyer’s litigation preparation is not automatically open to the opponent. Hickman recognized work-product protection even where attorney-client privilege did not apply.
steps.effect: Trial preparation is not automatically discoverable
steps.context: Witness statements, memoranda and mental impressions that a lawyer prepares in anticipation of litigation, though outside attorney-client privilege, cannot be obtained in discovery as of right; the party seeking them must show adequate reasons, such as necessity, for the intrusion.

steps.note: Corporate privilege can protect employees’ confidential communications with counsel beyond senior management. The Court separately gave strong protection to work product revealing counsel’s thinking.
steps.effect: Corporate privilege extends beyond top management
steps.context: Corporate attorney-client privilege is not limited to a control group: it protects confidential communications from employees to counsel, made at management's direction about matters within their duties, to obtain legal advice; work product revealing counsel's mental processes needs more than substantial need and undue hardship.

steps.note: An order requiring disclosure over an attorney-client privilege objection is not ordinarily an immediately appealable collateral order. Other review mechanisms remain available.
steps.effect: Privilege disclosure order lacks routine immediate appeal
steps.context: Disclosure orders adverse to the attorney-client privilege are not immediately appealable as collateral orders under 28 U.S.C. section 1291, because postjudgment review and other established mechanisms sufficiently protect the privilege.

timelines.guide: Attorney-client privilege protects qualifying confidential legal communications. Work product protects preparation for litigation. They are different protections with different limits. Hickman and Upjohn explain their scope; Mohawk asks when an order rejecting privilege can be appealed, not whether the communication is privileged.

timelines.title: Managing the case and sanctioning misconduct
timelines.question: What tools manage litigation, and what limits govern sanctions for noncompliance?
timelines.anchor: What tools manage litigation, and what limits govern sanctions for noncompliance?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: A management order can bind the parties even if its document has another title. Sanctions require attention to the particular rule or inherent power, the conduct and the procedure used. Under Goodyear’s civil inherent-power analysis, fee compensation must reflect costs caused by the misconduct.

steps.note: An auditor could organize complicated accounts and make tentative findings without replacing the jury’s final decision on disputed facts.
steps.effect: Auditor may assist while jury retains factfinding
steps.context: Absent contrary legislation, a federal court has inherent power to appoint an auditor without the parties' consent to clarify complicated accounts and make tentative findings, and doing so is consistent with the Seventh Amendment if the jury keeps the final determination of the facts.

steps.note: A signed pretrial report defining issues and witnesses functioned as a binding Rule 16 order regardless of its title. Last-minute changes were not automatic.
steps.effect: Substance makes the report a binding pretrial order
steps.context: A signed and filed pretrial report that defines the issues and lists the witnesses binds the parties at trial as a Rule 16 pretrial order whatever its title, and the trial judge has discretion to refuse amendments and a continuance sought at trial.

steps.note: Serious discovery sanctions could follow counsel’s grossly negligent disobedience, even without willfulness. Genuine inability to comply presented a different case.
steps.effect: Grossly negligent disobedience can justify severe sanctions
steps.context: Under Rule 37 a severe discovery sanction, such as precluding proof of damages, may be imposed for fault short of willfulness, including counsel's gross negligence in failing to obey discovery orders, though not for a genuine inability to comply.

steps.note: A party could be sanctioned for failing to prepare for and participate in good faith in court-ordered mediation, despite relying on its lawyer.
steps.effect: Bad-faith mediation participation can draw sanctions
steps.context: Rule 16(f) and a court's local rules authorize sanctions, including fines payable to the court and imposed on the party itself, for failing to prepare for and participate in good faith in court-ordered mediation, even where the party relied on its counsel.

steps.note: A compensatory fee sanction under inherent authority must track losses caused by the misconduct. It cannot become a punishment imposed through ordinary civil procedures.
steps.effect: Compensatory fees require misconduct-linked loss
steps.context: A fee award imposed under a federal court's inherent authority through civil procedures must be compensatory, not punitive: it is limited to the fees the innocent party would not have incurred but for the misconduct.

timelines.guide: Judges organize pretrial work and enforce orders, but their tools have limits. For each sanction, identify the source of power, the conduct at issue and the remedy imposed. A compensatory fee award repays losses caused by misconduct; a punishment raises different procedural questions.

timelines.title: The civil jury: which questions must jurors decide?
timelines.question: Which issues carry a civil jury right, and which remain for the judge?
timelines.anchor: Which issues carry a civil jury right, and which remain for the judge?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: The federal civil jury inquiry examines the claim, remedy and particular issue. Legal claims cannot lose their jury protection merely by being joined with equitable claims. Some tasks, such as patent-claim interpretation, remain for the judge. Bankruptcy and agency adjudication require their own constitutional analysis.

steps.note: An auditor could assist with complicated accounts while the jury retained the final word on factual disputes. Assistance was not a substitute for the jury.
steps.effect: Auditor assists without replacing jury
steps.context: Absent contrary legislation, a federal court has inherent power to appoint an auditor without the parties' consent to clarify complicated accounts and make tentative findings, and doing so is consistent with the Seventh Amendment if the jury keeps the final determination of the facts.

steps.note: A federal court’s interest in preserving its judge-jury division could outweigh a state practice not integral to the underlying state right.
steps.effect: Federal judge-jury allocation can outweigh state practice
steps.context: In diversity, a state rule on the mode of enforcing a state right that is not shown to be integral to that right yields to a strong countervailing federal interest, such as the federal judge-jury allocation, even though the outcome might differ.

steps.note: When legal and equitable claims shared factual issues, the trial sequence had to protect the jury’s decision on the legal claims rather than decide those facts first in equity.
steps.effect: Try shared legal issues before equitable resolution
steps.context: When legal and equitable claims in one action share common factual issues, the court's discretion over the order of trial must be used to preserve the jury right on the legal claim, which can be lost through a prior equitable determination only in the most imperative circumstances.

steps.note: Calling a damages claim incidental to equitable relief did not remove the jury right. Shared legal issues required jury resolution before final disposition of the equitable claims.
steps.effect: Equitable label cannot eliminate legal-issue jury right
steps.context: Where legal and equitable claims are joined, a timely jury demand on legal issues cannot be denied because those issues are called incidental to equitable ones, and legal issues must be tried to a jury before final disposition of equitable claims sharing them.

steps.note: For a shareholder derivative suit, ask whether the corporation would have had a jury right on the underlying issues had it brought the suit itself.
steps.effect: Derivative suit follows corporation’s underlying jury right
steps.context: The Seventh Amendment jury right extends to those issues in a shareholder derivative suit on which the corporation would have been entitled to a jury had it sued directly.

steps.note: A new statutory claim can carry a Seventh Amendment jury right when it enforces legal rights and seeks legal remedies, as this housing-discrimination damages claim did.
steps.effect: Statutory legal damages can carry a jury right
steps.context: The Seventh Amendment applies to statutory causes of action that enforce legal rights and seek legal remedies in the ordinary courts, so either party may demand a jury in a federal Title VIII action for actual and punitive damages.

steps.note: A defendant who had filed no bankruptcy claim retained a jury right when the trustee sought recovery of an allegedly fraudulent money transfer.
steps.effect: Fraudulent-transfer defendant retains jury right here
steps.context: A person who has filed no claim against a bankruptcy estate has a Seventh Amendment right to a jury when the trustee sues to recover an allegedly fraudulent transfer of money, even though Congress designated the action a core proceeding.

steps.note: The jury inquiry considers the historical nature of the action and, more importantly, the remedy. The requested union-duty damages counted as legal relief.
steps.effect: Nature of remedy carries greater weight
steps.context: The Seventh Amendment inquiry examines the nature of the action or issues and the nature of the remedy, giving greater importance to the remedy; damages sought from a union for breach of the duty of fair representation are legal relief triable to a jury.

steps.note: A judge interprets the patent’s claims. A jury right in the overall infringement action does not send every subsidiary issue to the jury.
steps.effect: Judge interprets patent claims
steps.context: Construction of a patent, including technical terms within its claims, is the exclusive responsibility of the court; the Seventh Amendment jury right attached to an infringement action does not make every subsidiary issue a jury question.

steps.note: The judge could screen and allow juror questions to witnesses. This concerns how to conduct a jury trial, not whether a jury right exists.
steps.effect: Screened juror questions concern trial administration
steps.context: The trial judge may permit jurors to submit witness questions while screening out irrelevant or argumentative questions. This concerns trial administration, not the existence of a jury right.

steps.note: The SEC’s civil-penalty fraud action required a jury in an Article III court. The public-rights exception did not permit the agency to decide this claim itself.
steps.effect: SEC fraud penalties require jury adjudication
steps.context: When the Government seeks civil penalties on a statutory claim that is legal in nature, such as securities fraud closely related to common-law fraud, the Seventh Amendment requires a jury trial in an Article III court unless the public-rights exception applies.

timelines.guide: The Seventh Amendment protects jury trial for certain civil disputes in federal court. Look at the kind of claim, the remedy and the particular issue—not just the lawsuit’s label. Some cases decide the jury’s role; others concern sequencing, bankruptcy, agency adjudication or the judge’s management of a jury trial.

timelines.title: Judgment as a matter of law: insufficient proof
timelines.question: When can the court remove a factual issue from the jury or overturn a verdict?
timelines.anchor: When can the court remove a factual issue from the jury or overturn a verdict?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: Rule 50 asks whether the fully heard party has a legally sufficient evidentiary basis for a reasonable jury to find in its favor. The judge cannot weigh credibility. A timely pre-verdict motion generally preserves a renewed post-verdict challenge; the ordinary renewal deadline is 28 days after judgment. Read the historical cases in light of that procedure.

steps.note: Under this historical reading of the Seventh Amendment, insufficient evidence required a new trial rather than appellate judgment replacing an unconditional jury verdict.
steps.fate: Historical 1913 rule; Redman and Rule 50 later permit judgment where the legal question was properly reserved.
steps.effect: Historical bar on replacing an unconditional verdict
steps.context: Under the Seventh Amendment's Reexamination Clause as read in 1913, an appellate court that finds the evidence insufficient may not enter judgment against an unconditional general jury verdict but must order a new trial.

steps.note: A judge could decide a previously reserved sufficiency motion after the verdict. Taking the verdict subject to that legal question preserved the constitutional distinction.
steps.effect: Reserved sufficiency question allows later judgment
steps.context: The Seventh Amendment permits judgment for a defendant after a plaintiff's jury verdict when the trial judge expressly reserved the defendant's sufficiency motions and took the verdict subject to their resolution.

steps.note: The jury need not decide an essential fact left to speculation. Directing a verdict on insufficient proof did not violate the Seventh Amendment.
steps.effect: Speculation does not require submission to jury
steps.context: Directing a verdict when the claimant's proof leaves an essential fact to speculation rather than reasonable inference does not violate the Seventh Amendment, which preserves the fundamental jury institution rather than every procedural detail.

steps.note: The causation evidence left the jury choosing among possibilities rather than drawing a supported inference. That speculation could not sustain the negligence verdict.
steps.effect: Speculative causation cannot sustain verdict
steps.context: A plaintiff must prove by a preponderance both negligence and its proximate contribution to the injury; a jury verdict cannot stand where the evidence leaves causation to speculation among possible explanations.

steps.note: Evidence undermining an employer’s explanation could support discrimination, but did not compel that conclusion. The judge reviewing sufficiency could not weigh credibility.
steps.effect: False explanation can support discrimination finding
steps.context: A prima facie case combined with sufficient evidence that the employer's stated justification is false may permit, but does not compel, an inference of intentional discrimination; under Rule 50 the court reviews the whole record without weighing evidence or resolving credibility.

timelines.guide: This motion asks whether a reasonable jury has enough evidence to find for a party. It does not ask the judge to choose which witness to believe. Follow the historical debate over entering judgment after a verdict, then the modern evidence standard and Rule 50’s preservation requirements.

reviewSources.label: Rule 50(a)–(b), (e); 1937 Advisory Committee Notes; Dupree, 598 U.S. 729

timelines.title: New trials and changes to damages awards
timelines.question: When may a judge order a new trial or adjust the consequences of a verdict?
timelines.anchor: When may a judge order a new trial or adjust the consequences of a verdict?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: A new-trial motion can address evidence weight and trial error, not just whether enough evidence exists. Federal and state damage-adjustment rules differ: Dimick bars federal additur of the kind it considered; Fisch approved New Jersey’s historical procedure, and Orientale later required both parties’ consent there. In diversity cases, Gasperini uses the state excessiveness standard through the federal trial judge, with appellate review for abuse of discretion.

steps.note: A judge deciding a new-trial motion may assess whether the verdict contradicts the clear weight of evidence. That is different from testing whether legally sufficient evidence exists.
steps.effect: New-trial review can consider evidence weight
steps.context: A motion for judgment notwithstanding the verdict tests legal sufficiency with the evidence viewed for the verdict winner, but on a new-trial motion the trial judge may set aside a verdict against the clear weight of the evidence, resting on false evidence, or producing a miscarriage of justice.

steps.note: Fisch approved New Jersey’s historical additur procedure, but found the increase inadequate and ordered a new damages trial. It did not authorize federal additur.
steps.effect: Historical New Jersey additur rule
steps.context: Fisch allowed the judge to condition a damages increase on the defendant’s consent. In Orientale (2019), New Jersey changed the procedure: both parties must accept the proposed additur or remittitur, or a new damages trial follows.
steps.fate: Procedure changed by Orientale v. Jennings (N.J. 2019): both parties must consent to additur or remittitur; otherwise a new damages trial is required.

reviewSources.label: Orientale v. Jennings (2019), opinion pp. 22–23 & n.8, 29–33

steps.note: In this case, liability and unliquidated damages were too connected to retry liability alone. The court required a new trial covering both.
steps.effect: Linked liability error can require retrial of all issues
steps.context: Because liability and damages are ordinarily intertwined, a new trial granted for an error affecting liability should extend to all issues where damages are unliquidated; a limited new trial is disfavored.

steps.note: The federal trial judge had to apply New York’s damages-excessiveness standard. The federal appellate court reviewed that decision for abuse of discretion.
steps.effect: Federal trial judge applies state damages standard
steps.context: In diversity, a state standard limiting the size of damages awards is substantive under Erie and must be applied, but by the federal district judge in the first instance, with the court of appeals reviewing only for abuse of discretion.

timelines.guide: A new trial sends issues back for another trial rather than entering judgment for the opponent. Compare insufficient proof with a verdict against the weight of evidence or tainted by error. Keep federal rules separate from state rules on additur—raising damages—and remittitur—reducing damages.

reviewSources.label: 293 U.S. 476–487; Gasperini, 518 U.S. 415; Fisch v. Manger, 24 N.J. 66
Orientale v. Jennings (2019), opinion pp. 22–23 & n.8, 29–33

timelines.title: Appeals: when can review begin?
timelines.question: When can an appellate court review a trial-court ruling before litigation ends?
timelines.anchor: When can an appellate court review a trial-court ruling before litigation ends?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: Final judgment is the ordinary starting point for appeal. Certified interlocutory review, collateral-order review and mandamus are separate exceptions with separate requirements. Resolving liability alone may not finish a claim; consolidating distinct lawsuits may still leave one finally decided action separately appealable.

steps.note: An appellate court could use exceptional mandamus review to correct improper wholesale referral to a master. Congestion and complexity did not justify that referral.
steps.effect: Mandamus corrects exceptional misuse of referral power
steps.context: A court of appeals that may eventually hear an appeal may issue mandamus under the All Writs Act in exceptional circumstances, and calendar congestion, complexity and trial length are not exceptional conditions permitting reference of a whole nonjury case to a master.

steps.note: The trial judge’s certification did not guarantee an immediate appeal. The appellate court could refuse review that would delay rather than advance the litigation.
steps.effect: Both courts must permit a certified early appeal
steps.context: A district court's certification under 28 U.S.C. § 1292(b) does not ensure an immediate appeal; the court of appeals may deny leave where early review would prolong rather than advance the litigation and the error can be corrected after final judgment.

steps.note: Deciding liability without resolving requested relief did not finish this single claim. Rule 54(b) could not turn that incomplete decision into a final judgment.
steps.effect: Liability-only ruling is not a complete final claim
steps.context: A determination of liability that leaves damages and other requested relief unresolved is interlocutory, and Rule 54(b) cannot make it a final decision, because a complaint asserting one legal right is a single claim even though it requests several remedies.

steps.note: Collateral-order review requires a conclusive decision on an important, separate issue that later appeal cannot effectively protect. A wish to avoid trial is not enough.
steps.effect: Collateral-order review has narrow requirements
steps.context: A collateral order must conclusively determine the disputed question, resolve an important issue completely separate from the merits, and be effectively unreviewable after final judgment; a claimed right to avoid trial qualifies only when delay would imperil a sufficiently substantial interest.

steps.note: An adverse attorney-client privilege ruling did not qualify for routine immediate appeal. Postjudgment review and other established procedures could protect the privilege.
steps.effect: Privilege order is reviewable through other routes
steps.context: Disclosure orders adverse to the attorney-client privilege are not immediately appealable as collateral orders under 28 U.S.C. section 1291, because postjudgment review and other established mechanisms sufficiently protect the privilege.

steps.note: Consolidated lawsuits kept their separate identities: a final judgment in one could be appealed while another continued.
steps.effect: One consolidated case’s final judgment can be appealed
steps.context: When one of several cases consolidated under Rule 42(a) is finally decided, the losing party may immediately appeal that decision under section 1291, because consolidation does not merge the constituent cases or eliminate their separate identities.

timelines.guide: Usually a party must wait for a final decision. These cases compare narrow routes to earlier review: a certified appeal, a collateral order or mandamus, an exceptional order directing the lower court. Also ask whether several joined proceedings still count as separate cases for appeal.

timelines.title: Appeals: who may challenge what?
timelines.question: What is reviewable, who may appeal, and which standard governs?
timelines.anchor: What is reviewable, who may appeal, and which standard governs?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: Identify the requested change to the judgment, the preserved issue and the standard of review. A party defending the existing judgment may offer another supported reason; seeking better relief generally requires a cross-appeal. Factfinding usually belongs below. Dupree’s preservation rule applies to purely legal summary-judgment issues.

steps.note: Winning ordinarily bars an appeal just to dispute unnecessary findings. But a winner could seek removal of an adverse adjudication written into the operative decree.
steps.effect: Prevailing party can challenge adverse operative decree
steps.context: A prevailing party ordinarily may not appeal a favorable judgment to challenge unnecessary findings, but may appeal to have an unnecessary adverse adjudication removed from the operative decree itself.

steps.note: This state decision allowed carefully limited appellate review of a verdict’s weight and a new trial. It did not announce a federal jury-review rule.
steps.effect: State law permits limited verdict-weight review
steps.context: A statute authorizing a reviewing court to set aside a verdict as against the manifest weight of the evidence and require a new jury trial does not violate the state constitutional right to jury trial, provided the power is exercised within strict limits.

steps.note: Discriminatory intent was a factual finding reviewed for clear error. Missing findings caused by legal error ordinarily required remand, not appellate factfinding.
steps.effect: Discriminatory intent is reviewed for clear error
steps.context: Rule 52(a)'s clearly erroneous standard governs a finding of discriminatory intent, with no exception for ultimate facts, and when a legal error has caused the trial court to omit findings the appellate court must ordinarily remand rather than find the facts itself.

steps.note: An appellee can defend the existing judgment on another supported ground. To obtain a more favorable judgment, the appellee generally needs a cross-appeal.
steps.effect: More favorable relief requires a cross-appeal
steps.context: An appellee may defend a judgment on any ground supported by the record, including one the trial court rejected, but must cross-appeal to enlarge its own rights or diminish the opponent's rights under that judgment.

steps.note: A purely legal issue rejected at summary judgment need not be renewed through Rule 50 to preserve appellate review. Fact-dependent sufficiency issues are different.
steps.effect: Pure legal issue needs no Rule 50 renewal
steps.context: A post-trial motion under Rule 50 is not required to preserve for appellate review a purely legal issue resolved at summary judgment.

timelines.guide: Once an appeal is available, ask who seeks a change, whether the argument was preserved, and how closely the appellate court may review the ruling. Defending an existing judgment differs from seeking more relief. Appellate judges also cannot freely replace trial judges’ factual findings with their own.

timelines.title: Claim preclusion: no second suit on the same claim
timelines.question: When does a final judgment block a second lawsuit about the same claim?
timelines.anchor: When does an earlier judgment require the plaintiff to bring the whole claim at once?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: First identify the law governing the earlier judgment’s effect. Then ask whether the second suit splits a claim that had to be resolved together. New damages requests or legal theories may belong to the same claim. Claim preclusion is broader than carrying forward only the issues actually decided.

steps.note: Using part of one indivisible demand to defeat an earlier lawsuit could prevent saving the rest for a later affirmative claim.
steps.effect: Using part of a demand may bar the remainder
steps.context: A party who knowingly uses part of an entire, indivisible demand as a defense to defeat an opponent's suit cannot reserve the remainder of that demand for a later affirmative action.

steps.note: Once acceleration made all installments due, the creditor had one debt claim. Taking judgment for only part prevented a later action on the rest.
steps.effect: Accelerated installments become one claim
steps.context: When an unconditional acceleration clause has made every installment of a note due, the debt is a single indivisible claim, and a creditor who takes judgment for only part of it cannot later sue for or rely on the remainder.

steps.note: Under this court’s claim definition, one wrong causing both injury and property loss created one claim. A judgment for one category of damages barred a second suit for the other.
steps.effect: Injury and property damages cannot be split here
steps.context: A single wrongful act that causes both personal injury and property damage to the same person gives rise to one cause of action with different items of damages, so a judgment on part of it bars a later action for the rest.

steps.note: Changing the legal theory did not create a new claim from the same transaction. The first judgment also protected principals whose liability derived from the previously sued agents.
steps.effect: New legal theory does not create a new transaction
steps.context: A claim consists of the facts of an occurrence or transaction, not the legal theory chosen, so a judgment on that transaction bars a later suit on new theories, including one against principals whose liability derives from the agents sued first.

steps.note: Federal law determines the effect of a federal diversity judgment, generally by borrowing the rendering state’s preclusion law. Rule 41(b) does not itself answer that question.
steps.effect: Federal diversity judgment borrows state preclusion rules
steps.context: Federal common law governs the claim-preclusive effect of a federal diversity judgment and ordinarily incorporates the preclusion law of the state where the federal court sat, unless that law is incompatible with a federal interest; Rule 41(b) does not itself prescribe that effect.

timelines.guide: After a binding final judgment, a party generally cannot split one claim into successive lawsuits. The governing law decides how broadly to define that claim. Compare splitting a debt, separating kinds of damages and changing legal theories. Semtek asks which law determines the first judgment’s effect.

timelines.title: Issue preclusion: no second decision of the same issue
timelines.question: When does an earlier determination bind later litigation, and who may invoke it?
timelines.anchor: When does an earlier determination bind later litigation, and who may invoke it?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: Identify the precise issue, its necessity to the earlier judgment and the affected party’s fair opportunity to litigate. Do not confuse a new claim with a new issue. Some courts permit a new party to invoke the earlier decision, but offensive use has additional fairness limits.

steps.note: A judgment bars the same claim broadly, but its effect on a different claim is narrower: only matters actually litigated and determined carry over.

reviewSources.label: Decision Date and Court Term fields

steps.effect: Same-claim bar differs from decided-issue preclusion
steps.context: A final judgment on the merits bars a later action on the same claim as to every ground that was or could have been raised, but in an action on a different claim it is conclusive only of matters actually litigated and determined.

steps.note: The party invoking issue preclusion must identify what the earlier judgment necessarily decided. Unresolved uncertainty between possible grounds defeats preclusion of a particular issue.

reviewSources.label: Decision Date and Court Term fields

steps.effect: Uncertain grounds do not establish a decided issue
steps.context: A party invoking a prior judgment as an estoppel must show, from the record or consistent extrinsic evidence, the precise question necessarily decided; if the judgment could rest on any of several distinct matters and the uncertainty is not removed, it is not conclusive of any one.

steps.note: California allowed a new litigant to invoke an earlier judgment against someone already bound by it. Strict mutuality—requiring both sides to have been bound—was unnecessary.
steps.effect: California rejects strict mutuality
steps.context: Mutuality is not required for issue preclusion: a judgment may be invoked by a stranger to it, so long as the issue is identical, the judgment was final on the merits, and the party against whom it is asserted was a party or privy.

steps.note: Each tax year is a separate claim. An earlier determination carries forward only for the same issue while the controlling facts and legal rules remain unchanged.
steps.effect: Changed facts or law can prevent tax-year estoppel
steps.context: Because each tax year is a separate claim, a prior tax judgment operates in a later year only as collateral estoppel, which requires an identical matter and unchanged controlling facts and legal rules.

steps.note: An unnecessary finding against the party who won the judgment did not bind that party later. It was not essential to the result and could not ordinarily be appealed.
steps.effect: Unnecessary adverse finding does not bind winner
steps.context: A finding in an earlier action does not bind a party in later litigation unless it was a material basis for the earlier judgment; a finding adverse to a party who won the judgment, and so could not appeal it, is not conclusive.

steps.note: New York required an identical, decisive issue previously resolved against a party who had a full and fair opportunity to contest it; the new claimants need not have participated earlier.
steps.effect: New York requires identical issue and fair opportunity
steps.context: Under New York's Schwartz formulation, a party is precluded from relitigating an identical issue that was necessarily decided earlier and is decisive now if that party had a full and fair opportunity to contest it, even when the present claimants were absent from the earlier action.

steps.note: A new patent defendant could invoke a previous invalidity judgment against the patentee, provided the patentee had a full and fair opportunity to litigate.
steps.effect: New defendant may invoke prior patent invalidity
steps.context: A defendant charged with infringing a patent previously declared invalid may plead that judgment as an estoppel against the patentee, even though the defendant was not a party to the first suit, unless the patentee shows it lacked a full and fair opportunity to litigate.

steps.note: A new plaintiff may sometimes use an earlier loss against a defendant. Federal trial judges retain discretion to reject that offensive use when joining earlier was easy or application would be unfair.
steps.effect: Offensive nonmutual use remains discretionary
steps.context: Federal trial courts have broad discretion to permit offensive nonmutual issue preclusion unless the plaintiff could easily have joined the earlier action or its use would be unfair to the defendant, and applying it to an issue decided in an equitable action does not violate the Seventh Amendment.

timelines.guide: Issue preclusion carries a decided issue into a later lawsuit, even when the new claim differs. Ask exactly what was decided, whether the decision was necessary, and whether the affected party had a fair chance to contest it. Later cases ask when someone new may invoke that decision.

timelines.title: When can a judgment bind someone who was absent?
timelines.question: When may a judgment affect someone who was not a party?
timelines.anchor: When may a judgment affect someone who was not a party?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: People ordinarily are not bound by litigation they did not join. Any exception needs a recognized basis, such as adequate representation; aligned interests alone are insufficient. A chance to intervene does not ordinarily create a duty. Certain employment-discrimination judgments have an additional statutory rule under § 2000e-2(n).

steps.note: Calling the first lawsuit a class action did not bind absent people whose interests were not adequately represented. Representation is a constitutional safeguard, not merely a label.
steps.effect: Class label cannot replace adequate representation
steps.context: Due process forbids binding a person to a judgment in an earlier representative action unless the parties to that action adequately represented that person's interests; a state's labelling a suit a class action does not settle its power to bind absentees.

steps.note: Knowing about a lawsuit and being able to intervene did not ordinarily bind an outsider who stayed out. Later legislation limits some employment-discrimination challenges.
steps.fate: Qualified for specified employment-discrimination judgments by the Civil Rights Act of 1991, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(n); the broader no-duty-to-intervene principle remains.
steps.effect: Outsider ordinarily has no duty to intervene
steps.context: A person is not bound by a judgment in litigation to which he was not a party; knowledge of the suit and a chance to intervene impose no duty to intervene, so parties who want to bind an outsider must join him.

steps.note: A settlement-only class still needed predominance and adequate representation of conflicting groups. A fair settlement could not substitute for those certification requirements.
steps.effect: Settlement class must protect conflicting interests
steps.context: A class certified only for settlement must still satisfy Rule 23(a) and (b), apart from trial manageability; the fairness of the settlement under Rule 23(e) cannot substitute for predominance of common questions and adequate representation of conflicting groups within the class.

steps.note: Shared interests or close relationships alone did not justify binding a nonparty. Preclusion required a recognized exception rather than open-ended “virtual representation.”
steps.effect: Virtual representation is not a free-ranging exception
steps.context: A person is ordinarily not bound by a judgment in litigation to which that person was not a party; nonparty preclusion must rest on an established ground, not on an open-ended virtual-representation balancing of relationships and aligned interests.

timelines.guide: The usual rule gives people their own opportunity to litigate. Recognized exceptions include adequate representation, such as a properly conducted class action. Knowing about a lawsuit does not ordinarily require intervention. Martin also has an important later statutory qualification for certain employment-discrimination judgments.

timelines.title: Judgments crossing state and federal court lines
timelines.question: Whose preclusion law governs when judgments move between state and federal courts?
timelines.anchor: Whose preclusion law governs when judgments move between state and federal courts?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: For a state judgment, § 1738 generally points federal courts to the rendering state’s preclusion rules. For a federal diversity judgment, Semtek uses federal common law that ordinarily borrows those state rules. The existence of a federal statute does not itself create a new cause of action to challenge conflicting judgments.

steps.note: A later federal § 1983 suit generally must respect the state judgment’s issue-preclusive effect, provided the affected party had a full and fair opportunity to litigate.
steps.effect: Federal § 1983 suit respects state issue preclusion
steps.context: Section 1983 does not displace conventional issue-preclusion principles or 28 U.S.C. § 1738; federal courts generally give a state judgment the preclusive effect the rendering state would, provided the party had a full and fair opportunity to litigate the issue.

steps.note: The federal custody statute did not create a private federal lawsuit to choose between conflicting state custody decrees. A federal statute does not automatically supply a federal remedy.
steps.effect: Custody statute creates no private federal remedy
steps.context: The Parental Kidnaping Prevention Act does not impliedly create a private federal cause of action to determine which of two conflicting state custody decrees is valid; whether a statute implies a remedy turns on congressional intent.

steps.note: The effect of a federal diversity judgment is governed by federal common law, ordinarily borrowing the preclusion rules of the state where that court sat.
steps.effect: Federal diversity judgment follows a distinct route
steps.context: Federal common law governs the claim-preclusive effect of a federal diversity judgment and ordinarily incorporates the preclusion law of the state where the federal court sat, unless that law is incompatible with a federal interest; Rule 41(b) does not itself prescribe that effect.

timelines.guide: Start with the court that issued the first judgment. A state judgment and a federal diversity judgment reach the next court through different legal rules. Then ask what preclusive effect the governing law gives that judgment. Thompson separately asks whether Congress created a federal lawsuit to resolve conflicting custody decrees.

timelines.title: When courts may hear disputes about government power
timelines.question: Is there an injured plaintiff and a legal standard a court can apply?
timelines.anchor: Which constitutional disputes may courts decide, and who has the injury needed to bring them?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: Ask both whether the plaintiff has the required injury and whether the issue has a judicially manageable legal standard. A legislator’s generalized loss of influence differs from a legislature’s or committee’s own injury. A vacated judgment remains historical material, not an operative precedent.

steps.note: Courts may enforce specific legal duties affecting individual rights and must follow the Constitution over a conflicting statute. Political discretion presents a different kind of question.
steps.effect: Distinguishes judicially enforceable duties from discretion

steps.note: An abstract reduction in Congress’s power did not give these individual legislators standing. A statutory invitation to sue could not supply the missing personal injury.
steps.effect: Rejects the individual legislators’ standing claim

steps.note: The state legislature could assert its own institutional injury. On the merits, “Legislature” included the state’s lawmaking process, including the people acting by initiative.
steps.effect: Recognizes the legislature’s own institutional injury

steps.note: The Court found no judicially manageable constitutional standard for deciding how much partisan advantage is too much. Federal courts therefore could not decide these partisan-gerrymandering claims.
steps.effect: Leaves partisan-fairness claims outside federal court

steps.note: The D.C. Circuit distinguished a chamber’s own appropriations power from an ordinary objection that the Executive violated a statute. Its institutional-standing judgment was later vacated.
steps.fate: The 2020 judgment was later vacated; read the assigned account as historical institutional-standing analysis.
steps.effect: Historically recognizes one chamber’s spending injury

steps.note: The authorized House committee alleged its own concrete injury when an executive official withheld subpoenaed testimony. That supported Article III standing; standing alone did not resolve every obstacle to enforcement.
steps.effect: Recognizes the authorized committee’s subpoena injury

timelines.guide: Two different barriers appear here. Standing asks whether the plaintiff has its own concrete injury; political-question doctrine asks whether the issue is one a court may decide. Individual legislators, a whole legislature, and an authorized committee are different plaintiffs. Read historical lower-court rulings with their later procedural treatment.

timelines.title: Hearing rights created by an agency’s statute
timelines.question: Who may participate, and what evidence must they be able to challenge?
timelines.anchor: Who is entitled to an agency hearing, and what procedural protection does the statute supply?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: The statute and the type of proceeding determine who gets to participate and how. A comparative licensing hearing, public participation, and the ability to test evidence serve different purposes. None can be reduced to a universal requirement of live courtroom-style testimony.

steps.note: Two genuine broadcast applications could not both be granted. Hearing only the first before granting it would empty the second applicant’s statutory hearing right, so both required consideration.
steps.effect: Requires a hearing for both competing applicants

steps.note: Listeners’ representatives could participate in license renewal, subject to agency control of the proceeding. The FCC needed a hearing when it could not otherwise make the required public-interest finding.
steps.effect: Allows listener participation in license renewal

steps.note: Written reports by examining doctors could support the benefits decision despite hearsay and conflicting live testimony. The claimant had not used the available right to subpoena the doctors.
steps.effect: Accepts written medical evidence with subpoena safeguards

steps.note: The Natural Gas Act did not reach liquid petroleum. For rates it did cover, substantial-evidence review required a record whose factual basis parties could meaningfully test, without necessarily using full formal APA procedures.
steps.effect: Requires an opportunity to test the factual record

timelines.guide: A statute can require a hearing even when the Constitution does not require an individualized hearing. Compare competing license applicants, members of the listening public, a disability claimant, and parties contesting rates. The hearing’s purpose and the governing statute determine the opportunity required; a hearing does not always require live testimony.

timelines.title: Literal wording, apparent mistakes, and later amendments
timelines.question: When may a court depart from an apparent literal reading, and when must Congress fix the words?
timelines.anchor: When do courts read beyond literal wording, and how can legislation change the result?
timelines.up: Broadens the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.down: Limits the protection or route identified in the note
timelines.now: Purpose and context sometimes narrow literal wording, but courts disagree about correcting apparent drafting errors. Preserve the difference between an interpretation of old text and Congress’s later amendment. The CAFA steps do not state the current appeal deadline.

steps.note: The Court excluded the foreign-pastor contract from the labor statute despite its broad words. It relied on the enactment’s setting, purpose, and consequences.
steps.effect: Excludes the pastor’s contract despite broad wording

steps.note: The court read the jury-service statute in its historical setting and declined to extend it to women when they later gained voting rights. This is a historical interpretation, not a statement of current jury eligibility.
steps.effect: Historically excludes women from this jury statute

steps.note: The Court narrowed “utilized” to avoid an implausibly broad reading and serious constitutional concerns. The Justice Department’s use of the ABA committee therefore fell outside FACA.
steps.effect: Narrows “utilized” in the advisory-committee statute

steps.note: The court treated the former CAFA appeal language as a clear drafting error and read “not less than” seven days as “not more than” seven days. Congress later changed the text.
steps.fate: Historical CAFA wording. Congress later amended the text; this is not the current appeal deadline.
steps.effect: Corrects apparent error in the former appeal text
steps.context: CAFA is the Class Action Fairness Act. This decision addresses an earlier version of its appeal language. The historical disagreement is useful for statutory interpretation, not as instructions for a current filing.

steps.note: The court would not reject an application that complied with the former statute’s actual words merely because they appeared mistaken. It used appellate rules where the text supplied no final deadline; the statute was later amended.
steps.fate: Historical CAFA wording. Congress later amended the text; this is not the current appeal deadline.
steps.effect: Protects an application complying with the former text
steps.context: Compare the previous step: the courts responded differently to the apparent drafting error. Congress later amended the wording, so keep the old-text dispute separate from the current statute.

timelines.guide: Separate interpretation from amendment. These historical cases disagree about when context, purpose, or an apparent drafting mistake permits a narrower or corrected reading. The two CAFA decisions concern old appeal language that Congress later changed. Their disagreement illustrates the problem; neither supplies the current filing deadline.

timelines.title: Who owns the claim, and who may join the case?
timelines.question: Who owns the claim, who may enter the suit, and must outsiders intervene?
timelines.anchor: who may litigate a claim or enter litigation
timelines.now: Identify who owns the substantive claim before deciding who should sue. Intervention asks a different question: whether an outsider may enter to protect an interest. Permission to intervene ordinarily does not require intervention, subject to recognized preclusion exceptions and the statutory qualification noted under Martin.

steps.note: Under Kansas law, an insurer that fully paid the loss owned the subrogated claim and had to sue in its own name; the insured no longer owned that claim.
steps.effect: Fully paid loss puts claim in insurer’s hands
steps.context: Under the Kansas real-party-in-interest statute, once an insurer has fully paid a loss the subrogated claim belongs wholly to the insurer, which must bring the action in its own name; the insured cannot sue for the insurer's benefit.

steps.note: The plurality allowed intervention to protect inadequately represented interests, but only to challenge parts of the decree that actually affected those interests.
steps.effect: Plurality permits intervention to protect affected interests
steps.context: On a three-judge plurality's analysis, a person whose practical interest may be impaired and inadequately represented by existing parties can intervene under Rule 24(a)(2), even to appeal after judgment, but only to challenge decree provisions that actually affect that interest.

steps.note: An outsider ordinarily need not intervene simply to avoid being bound by the judgment. Martin’s employment-discrimination setting later received a statutory qualification.
steps.fate: Qualified for specified employment-discrimination judgments by the Civil Rights Act of 1991, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-2(n); the broader no-duty-to-intervene principle remains.
steps.effect: Opportunity to intervene creates no general duty
steps.context: A person is not bound by a judgment in litigation to which he was not a party; knowledge of the suit and a chance to intervene impose no duty to intervene, so parties who want to bind an outsider must join him.

timelines.guide: A real party in interest is the person entitled to enforce the claim. Intervention lets an outsider enter an existing case to protect an interest. Those are different questions. The opportunity to intervene also does not ordinarily mean the outsider must intervene to avoid being bound.
